| 10.1.6 | A-10.1.6-CL40 | exception | core | When a user exception-handler handles the nonfatal exception 1506 raised by a READ of an underflowing numeric datum, the READ does not complete: the variable keeps its value (zero is not supplied) and the handler receives the exception. | PRT-0410 |
| 10.2 | E-1507 | exception | core | An implementation may raise nonfatal exception 1507 for a numeric input underflow (supply zero and continue), so a handler can intercept it. | PRT-0047 |
| 10.2.2 | A-10.2.2-01 | syntax | core | An input-modifier-list may hold at most one PROMPT, one TIMEOUT and one ELAPSED, in any order. | PRT-0026 |
| 10.2.2 | A-ECMA-26 | semantics | core | INPUT with lists and PROMPT, INPUT with TIMEOUT, ELAPSED and PROMPT, LINE INPUT and its PROMPT form, and the shown reply forms all work. | ECMA-0055, ECMA-0056, ECMA-0057, ECMA-0058 |
| 10.2.3 | A-10.2.3-EX | semantics | core | Every INPUT and LINE INPUT form shown in the examples of section 10.2.3 is accepted and behaves as written. | PRT-0027 |
| 10.2.4 | A-10.2.4-01 | semantics | core | An INPUT halts the program until a valid input-reply arrives, then assigns the listed variables, left to right, from that reply. | PRT-0028 |
| 10.2.4.1 | A-10.2.4.1-01 | semantics | core | With a PROMPT specifier the built-in prompt is suppressed and the given string is printed instead, unless the reply ends with a comma. | PRT-0029 |
| 10.2.4.1 | A-10.2.4.1-02 | semantics | core | A TIMEOUT expression is evaluated to a number S of seconds; if no valid reply arrives within S an exception occurs, and ELAPSED stores the seconds elapsed between the prompt and the end-of-line of the last reply. | PRT-0030 |
| 10.2.4.1 | A-10.2.4.1-03 | semantics | core | Without a clock, TIMEOUT does nothing and ELAPSED yields -1; with a clock, an ELAPSED result is always positive. | PRT-0031 |
| 10.2.4.1 | A-10.2.4.1-TR84 | semantics | core | The numeric-variable of a time-inquiry may be an array element (also with a variable subscript or in two dimensions): ELAPSED E(2) in INPUT, LINE INPUT, MAT INPUT and MAT LINE INPUT assigns the positive time to that element and leaves the other elements unchanged. | PRT-0260 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-01 | semantics | core | Each variable receives its value as soon as the corresponding reply datum passes the type and range checks. | PRT-0032 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-02 | semantics | core | Subscripts and substring qualifiers in an INPUT list are evaluated only after the variables to their left received their values. | PRT-0033 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-03 | semantics | core | Reply data must match variable types: numeric constants for numeric variables, quoted or unquoted strings for string variables; an unquoted string that also parses as a number may fill either. | PRT-0034 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-04 | semantics | core | A numeric input datum that underflows is stored as zero. | PRT-0035 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-05 | semantics | core | When no reply ends with a comma, the total number of data across all replies must equal the number of variables. | PRT-0036 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-06 | semantics | core | A comma as the last non-blank character of a reply means more data follow: the values present are assigned, the built-in prompt is shown again (not a PROMPT string), and the program waits for the next reply. | PRT-0037 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-07 | semantics | core | LINE INPUT asks for one whole line per string variable: the first line goes to the first variable, the prompt is reissued for each further variable, until every variable got a line. | PRT-0038 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-08 | semantics | core | A line reply is stored verbatim, keeping leading and trailing spaces but dropping the end-of-line; quote characters inside are literal, so two adjacent quotes stay two characters. | PRT-0039 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-09 | semantics | core | When INPUT (or INPUT #0) raises 8002, 8103 or 1007 after earlier data of the same input-reply were validated, those data remain assigned to their variables; the exception is raised after them. | PRT-0144, PRT-0145, PRT-0146, PRT-0149, PRT-0152 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-10 | exception | core | When an input-reply ending in a comma is continued by further replies, the total number of data must equal the number of variables; extra data raise nonfatal 8003 after the variables were assigned. | PRT-0154 |
| 10.2.4.2 | A-10.2.4.2-CL11 | semantics | core | An input-reply whose final non-space character is a comma continues on another reply, even when spaces follow that comma: INPUT and MAT INPUT assign the values read so far and ask for another reply. A comma inside a quoted string is not a continuation. | PRT-0406 |
| 10.2.5 | E-1007 | exception | core | An overflow while evaluating a numeric datum typed at the terminal raises nonfatal exception 1007, which asks to resupply the current reply: when it is not the first reply of the statement (a continuation after a final comma, also in MAT INPUT) only that reply is asked again and the data of the earlier replies stay assigned. | PRT-0044, PRT-0201 |
| 10.2.5 | E-1054 | exception | core | A string datum or line reply that overflows its string variable raises nonfatal exception 1054, which asks to resupply the reply; the code is the same when the target is a substring (10.2.4.2 l.5186-5190) or a by-reference string parameter whose argument has a smaller length-max (9.2.4.1 l.4679-4682), or an element of a string array with a length-max (also in MAT INPUT and MAT LINE INPUT, 10.5.5 l.6130-6132); when it is not the first reply of the statement (a continuation after a final comma, the second reply of LINE INPUT, the second or later line of MAT LINE INPUT) only that reply is asked again and the data of the earlier replies stay assigned. | PRT-0045, PRT-0171, PRT-0172, PRT-0180, PRT-0190, PRT-0202 |
| 10.2.5 | E-8002 | exception | core | Fewer data than variables in a reply that does not end with a comma raises nonfatal exception 8002, which asks to resupply the current reply. | PRT-0042, PRT-0251 |
| 10.2.5 | E-8003 | exception | core | More data than variables, or exactly enough data followed by a final comma, raises nonfatal exception 8003, which asks to resupply the current reply. | PRT-0043, PRT-0252, PRT-0253, PRT-0254 |
| 10.2.5 | E-8102 | exception | core | A terminal line that is not a syntactically valid input-reply raises nonfatal exception 8102, which asks for a fresh reply (INPUT, MAT INPUT). | PRT-0040, PRT-0250 |
| 10.2.5 | E-8103 | exception | core | A datum supplied for a numeric variable that is not a numeric constant raises nonfatal exception 8103, which asks to resupply the current reply: when it is not the first reply of the statement (a continuation after a final comma, also in MAT INPUT) only that reply is asked again and the data of the earlier replies stay assigned. | PRT-0041, PRT-0200 |
| 10.2.5 | E-8402 | exception | core | A TIMEOUT whose numeric expression is negative raises fatal exception 8402, also in the input statements for channel zero (INPUT #0, LINE INPUT #0, 11.4.4.6 l.8205-8209). | PRT-0046, PRT-0203, PRT-0204 |
| 10.3.2 | A-10.3.2-01 | syntax | core | Each ask-io-item (MARGIN or ZONEWIDTH) may appear at most once in one ASK statement. | PRT-0051 |
| 10.3.2 | A-ECMA-27 | semantics | core | PRINT with single items, comma lists, trailing comma, leading commas, empty PRINT, literals and TAB, plus SET MARGIN and SET ZONEWIDTH with ASK, work as written. | ECMA-0059, ECMA-0060 |
| 10.3.3 | A-10.3.3-EX | semantics | core | Every PRINT, SET MARGIN and SET ZONEWIDTH form shown in the examples of section 10.3.3 is accepted and behaves as written. | PRT-0052 |
| 10.3.4 | A-10.3.4-01 | semantics | core | A PRINT builds the character string and line breaks sent to the output device by evaluating each item and separator of its print-list in order. | PRT-0053 |
| 10.3.4.1 | A-10.3.4.1-01 | semantics | core | A printed number becomes a leading space (positive value) or minus sign (negative value), the decimal form of its magnitude, and one trailing space. | PRT-0054 |
| 10.3.4.1 | A-10.3.4.1-02 | semantics | core | The printing precision d and the exrad width e chosen by the implementation are at least 6 and 2 respectively. | PRT-0055 |
| 10.3.4.1 | A-10.3.4.1-03 | semantics | core | A value that is an exact integer representable with d or fewer digits is printed without a decimal point. | PRT-0056 |
| 10.3.4.1 | A-10.3.4.1-04 | semantics | core | All other values print either in plain decimal or in scaled form; when d digits in plain decimal are at least as accurate, the plain form is chosen. | PRT-0057 |
| 10.3.4.1 | A-10.3.4.1-05 | semantics | core | Plain decimal form carries up to d significant digits and a period; trailing zeros of the fraction may be dropped, and a magnitude below 1 prints no digit left of the period. | PRT-0058 |
| 10.3.4.1 | A-10.3.4.1-06 | semantics | core | Scaled form prints significand, letter E, sign and exponent; the significand lies in [1,10) with exactly d digits, the exponent uses one to e digits, and removable zeros may be dropped. | PRT-0059 |
| 10.3.4.1 | A-10.3.4.1-07 | semantics | core | Only a value that is exactly an integer prints without a period; a non-integer value whose rounding to d digits leaves no fraction still prints with an explicit period (3., 12345679.), unless it needs the scaled form. | PRT-0262, PRT-0263 |
| 10.3.4.2 | A-10.3.4.2-01 | semantics | core | A string item of a print-list is printed as the string its expression evaluates to. | PRT-0060 |
| 10.3.4.3 | A-10.3.4.3-01 | semantics | core | A comma separator evaluated in the last print zone of a line generates an end-of-line, so the next print item starts a new line. The runner ignores trailing blanks, so this program fixes the line break, not the absence of padding after the last item. | PRT-0004 |
| 10.3.4.3 | A-10.3.4.3-02 | semantics | core | A semicolon separator emits the empty string. | PRT-0061 |
| 10.3.4.3 | A-10.3.4.3-03 | semantics | core | Columns are numbered from one at the left; each character printed advances the column by one, and each end-of-line resets it to one. | PRT-0062 |
| 10.3.4.3 | A-10.3.4.3-04 | semantics | core | The margin caps the column a character may occupy; a margin of MAXNUM removes the cap, and the default margin before any SET MARGIN is at least the default zone width. | PRT-0063, PRT-0064 |
| 10.3.4.3 | A-10.3.4.3-05 | semantics | core | A print line is split into equal-width zones (the last one may be shorter), and the default zone width is at least d+e+6 columns. | PRT-0065, PRT-0066 |
| 10.3.4.3 | A-10.3.4.3-06 | semantics | core | TAB rounds its argument to the nearest integer n; n below one raises an exception, and n above the margin m wraps by whole margins into the range 1 to m. | PRT-0067 |
| 10.3.4.3 | A-10.3.4.3-07 | semantics | core | TAB then pads with spaces up to column n, or, when the current column is already past n, emits an end-of-line followed by n-1 spaces. | PRT-0068 |
| 10.3.4.3 | A-10.3.4.3-08 | semantics | core | A comma separator moves to the start of the next zone on the line; when already in the last zone, or beyond the margin, it emits an end-of-line instead. | PRT-0069 |
| 10.3.4.4 | A-10.3.4.4-01 | semantics | core | An item that would cross the margin starts on a fresh line; while an item is being printed, any character that would land beyond the margin triggers an end-of-line first. | PRT-0070 |
| 10.3.4.5 | A-10.3.4.5-01 | semantics | core | When a print-list finishes without a trailing separator, a final end-of-line is emitted; with a trailing separator, none is. | PRT-0071, PRT-0158, PRT-0159, PRT-0160 |
| 10.3.4.5 | A-10.3.4.5-02 | semantics | core | A PRINT with an empty list emits an end-of-line, which yields a blank line when nothing else was on the current line. | PRT-0072 |
| 10.3.4.6 | A-10.3.4.6-01 | semantics | core | SET MARGIN evaluates its index and applies the new margin at once, even on a half-filled line; it affects only unformatted output. | PRT-0073 |
| 10.3.4.7 | A-10.3.4.7-01 | semantics | core | SET ZONEWIDTH evaluates its index and applies the new zone width at once, even on a half-filled line; it affects only unformatted output. | PRT-0074 |
| 10.3.4.8 | A-10.3.4.8-01 | semantics | core | ASK MARGIN and ASK ZONEWIDTH store the current margin or zone width in their variables; ASK MARGIN yields MAXNUM when the column may grow without bound. | PRT-0075 |
| 10.3.5 | A-10.3.5-CL40 | exception | core | When a user exception-handler handles the nonfatal exception 4005 raised by a TAB whose index is less than one, the print statement does not complete and the handler receives the exception; a RETRY in the handler runs the statement again. | PRT-0408 |
| 10.3.5 | A-10.3.5-EXC | exception | core | SET MARGIN below the current zone width raises fatal exception 4006, and SET ZONEWIDTH below one or above the current margin raises fatal exception 4007 (the Table 9 entries are covered by E-4006 and E-4007). | PRT-0076, PRT-0077, PRT-0078, PRT-0412 |
| 10.3.5 | E-4005 | exception | core | A TAB whose index is less than one raises the nonfatal exception 4005 with the index replaced by one; without a handler the report names the code and line and execution continues, and a handler can intercept it. | PRT-0001, PRT-0002 |
| 10.4.2 | A-10.4.2-01 | syntax | core | A PRINT USING whose format is given by line number may only name an IMAGE line that belongs to the program-unit containing the statement, so naming one that lives in a different program-unit is rejected before the program runs. | PRT-0005, PRT-0006 |
| 10.4.2 | A-10.4.2-02 | semantics | core | A PRINT USING that names an IMAGE line of its own program-unit (the main program, an internal subprogram of it, or an external subprogram) uses that line as its format. | PRT-0007 |
| 10.4.2 | A-10.4.2-03 | semantics | core | A PRINT USING may name an IMAGE line that follows it in the same program-unit; the standard imposes no order between the two, and this holds inside external subprograms and external functions as well as in the main program. | PRT-0008 |
| 10.4.2 | A-10.4.2-04 | syntax | core | All digit places of an i-format-item use one and the same fill character: number signs, percent signs or asterisks; a run of different digit places is split into several format-items (the longest correct one is taken, 10.4.4.1), and a text with no valid reading, such as "#,%", raises 8201 when the PRINT USING runs. | PRT-0087 |
| 10.4.2 | A-10.4.2-05 | syntax | core | A justifier on its own is a valid format-item of width 1, so a format string made of one justifier is not invalid (no 8201); a string longer than that field raises the nonfatal 8203. | PRT-0153 |
| 10.4.2 | A-10.4.2-TR109 | semantics | core | An image-line inside an internal SUB or FUNCTION is an image-line of its program unit: a PRINT USING line-number in the main or in another routine of the unit, above or below it, uses it. | PRT-0307 |
| 10.4.2 | A-10.4.2-TR118 | semantics | core | An image-line nested in a block (the USE part of a when-use-block, an if-block) is an image-line of its program unit: a PRINT USING line-number placed above it, including one in the same when-block, uses it. | PRT-0310 |
| 10.4.2 | A-ECMA-28 | semantics | core | PRINT USING with an inline format and with an IMAGE line reproduces the output cited by the ECMA examples. | ECMA-0061, ECMA-0062 |
| 10.4.3 | A-10.4.3-EX | semantics | core | The PRINT USING examples of section 10.4.3 run and produce exactly the output shown for them. | PRT-0088, PRT-0089, PRT-0139, PRT-0141 |
| 10.4.4.1 | A-10.4.4.1-01 | semantics | core | A format-string is scanned left to right into format-items separated by literal runs (possibly empty); at each position the longest valid format-item starting there wins, and scanning resumes just past it. | PRT-0090 |
| 10.4.4.1 | A-10.4.4.1-02 | semantics | core | Every format-item owns an output field as wide as the item itself, counting justifier, floating characters, digit places, commas, period, signs and circumflex accents; characters outside items are literal text. | PRT-0091 |
| 10.4.4.1 | A-10.4.4.1-03 | semantics | core | A format-string taken from an IMAGE line is read up to the last character that is not a space. | PRT-0092 |
| 10.4.4.1 | A-10.4.4.1-TR174 | semantics | core | The format-string is scanned from left to right and at each point the longest syntactically correct format-item is taken, the next search starting right after it. Format-items written one against the other are therefore separate fields: "##-##-####" is "##", "-##" and "-####" (12, 5, 1983 print as 12  5 1983), "#.#.#" is "#.#" and ".#", and "##$##" is "##" and "$##". A comma, sign, dollar sign or period left over after a format-item is not a literal-item (production 8 of 10.4.2 lists them closed), so the format-string is invalid (8201, fatal), as is an e-format with one or two circumflex accents. | PRT-0397, PRT-0398, PRT-0399, PRT-0400, PRT-0401 |
| 10.4.4.2 | A-10.4.4.2-01 | semantics | core | The output-list expressions are evaluated in sequence; before each one the literal run preceding its format-item is copied verbatim, then the field is produced by the numeric or string rules. | PRT-0093 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-01 | semantics | core | Numeric output is rounded to fit its format-item; a justifier character is replaced by the character on its right, or by a number sign when that is a period or missing. | PRT-0094 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-02 | semantics | core | An i-format-item rounds the value to a whole number and prints it in implicit-point form. | PRT-0095 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-03 | semantics | core | An f-format-item prints explicit-point form, rounding or padding with zeros to match the number signs that follow the period. | PRT-0096 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-04 | semantics | core | For i- and f-items no leading zeros appear left of the point unless that would print no digit at all (then one 0); leftover places are then filled with zeros for percent places, asterisks for asterisk places or spaces for number signs, until the integer part spans all digit places. | PRT-0097 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-05 | semantics | core | An e-format-item prints scaled form, f-style or i-style as its inner item dictates; the significand is shifted so its leftmost place holds a nonzero digit, and the exponent field takes as many characters as there are circumflex accents: letter E, a mandatory sign (plus when the exponent is zero) and the exponent magnitude zero-padded to that width. | PRT-0098 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-06 | semantics | core | Commas from the format-item are copied into the number wherever a digit already stands left of the insertion point; otherwise an asterisk (asterisk place to the left) or a space (number sign to the left) is printed. | PRT-0140 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-07 | semantics | core | Leading sign, dollar and space characters follow the table of floating characters, and the finished number is padded on the left with spaces until it fills the whole field, right-justified. | PRT-0099 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-08 | semantics | core | Floating-character runs fill the field width per the table (-- pads with a leading space, $$ (several $, no trailing sign) pads with $ for non-negative and $- for negative, the $ adjacent to the digits, per the table on p.126 of the printed standard (l.5767-5775 of the transcription are garbled) and field width = every character of the format-item (l.5688-5692); integer digits may overflow the digit-places into the floating room (10.4.6 l.5859-5862: $$## of 123 is $123); an f-format-item with no integer digit-places prints no leading zero (.## of .5 is .50, of 0 is .00), an unfilled number-sign place left of the point prints a space (#.## of .5 is  .50), and an e-format significand is scaled so the leftmost integer digit-place holds a nonzero digit (###^^^^ of 12345 is 123E+02). | PRT-0142 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-09 | semantics | core | Leading zeros generated by a percent-sign place count as generated numerals, so a comma to their right is inserted (%,%%% of 12 is 0,012; of 0 is 0,000; %,%%,%%% of 12 is 0,00,012), also after a floating dollar sign and in f-format-items; only asterisk and number-sign places replace a comma by their fill character when nothing precedes it (#,### of 12 is blank-filled, *,*** of 12 is ***12). Agreed interpretation of 10.4.4.3 (interpretations.yaml). | PRT-0161 |
| 10.4.4.3 | A-10.4.4.3-TR175 | semantics | core | With floating-characters that start with a plus-sign and end with a dollar-sign the leading characters are "+$" for a non-negative value and "-$" for a negative one, with no space before them: "+$##.##" prints 12.5 as +$12.50 and -12.5 as -$12.50, and "+$###.##" prints 1.5 as +$  1.50. With two plus-signs ("++$##") the extra plus-sign provides the room and the output is the same two rows, right-justified in the field. | PRT-0402, PRT-0403 |
| 10.4.4.4 | A-10.4.4.4-01 | semantics | core | A string printed through any format-item is padded with spaces to the field width: on the left when the item starts with >, on the right when it starts with <, split evenly otherwise with an odd extra space on the right. | PRT-0100 |
| 10.4.4.4 | A-10.4.4.4-02 | exception | core | A string longer than its format-item raises nonfatal exception 8203: the field fills with asterisks and the unformatted string is reported on the next line. | PRT-0143 |
| 10.4.4.5 | A-10.4.4.5-01 | semantics | core | When there are more values than format-items, an end-of-line is emitted each time the format-string is exhausted and it is reused; unused trailing items still emit their following literal text, and output stops at the first unused item. | PRT-0101 |
| 10.4.4.5 | A-10.4.4.5-02 | semantics | core | After all formatted output a final end-of-line is emitted, unless the output-list ends with a semicolon. | PRT-0102 |
| 10.4.4.5 | A-10.4.4.5-03 | semantics | core | The current margin never wraps formatted output, and reaching an IMAGE line at run time just continues with the next line. | PRT-0103, PRT-0411 |
| 10.4.5 | A-10.4.5-CL10 | exception | core | After a nonfatal 8203 the output is three lines: the text so far with the field filled with asterisks; the unformatted value on the next line; and whatever remains to be printed on the line after that, starting at the column it would have had if the exception had not occurred (the column that follows the field). The rule is the same for numbers and strings, for the first, an intermediate or the last field, and for a record of a DISPLAY file written by PRINT # USING, where each of the three lines is one record. | PRT-0405 |
| 10.4.5 | A-10.4.5-CL29 | exception | core | When a PRINT # USING statement writes to a DISPLAY file whose current record was left open by an earlier PRINT # ending in a print-separator, the characters it generates are appended to that partial record and every column it counts, including the column at which the output continues after a nonfatal 8203, is measured from the start of that record exactly as it is on the console. | PRT-0407 |
| 10.4.5 | E-8201 | exception | core | A malformed format-string in PRINT USING or MAT PRINT USING raises fatal exception 8201. | PRT-0104 |
| 10.4.5 | E-8202 | exception | core | An output list whose format-string contains no format-item raises fatal exception 8202. | PRT-0105 |
| 10.4.5 | E-8203 | exception | core | A value longer than its format-item raises nonfatal exception 8203: the field fills with asterisks and the plain value is reported on the next line. | PRT-0106, PRT-0143 |
| 10.4.5 | E-8204 | exception | core | An exponent too large for the circumflex accents of an e-format-item raises nonfatal exception 8204, filling the field with asterisks and reporting the plain value. | PRT-0107 |
| 10.5.2 | A-10.5.2-01 | syntax | core | A redim attached to an array in MAT READ or MAT INPUT must state the same number of dimensions as the array. | PRT-0108 |
| 10.5.2 | A-10.5.2-02 | syntax | core | A variable-length vector (the question-mark form) is always one-dimensional. | PRT-0109 |
| 10.5.2 | A-10.5.2-TR94 | syntax | files | The number of bounds in a redim attached to an array in MAT INPUT #, MAT LINE INPUT # or MAT READ # must equal the number of dimensions of that array (rule of 10.5.2 reused by 11.4.2); it is checked when the program is loaded, as it already was for the console forms, whenever the dimensionality of the array is known. | ARR-0242, ARR-0243, ARR-0244 |
| 10.5.2 | A-ECMA-29 | semantics | core | MAT READ (with redims), MAT INPUT (fixed redim, ? redim, PROMPT), MAT LINE INPUT and MAT PRINT with mixed separators work as written. | ECMA-0063, ECMA-0064, ECMA-0065, ECMA-0066 |
| 10.5.3 | A-10.5.3-EX | semantics | core | Every MAT statement form shown in the examples of section 10.5.3 is accepted and behaves as written. | PRT-0110 |
| 10.5.4.1 | A-10.5.4.1-01 | semantics | core | MAT READ fills the listed arrays in order from the data sequence of its unit, covering every element row by row (last subscript fastest) and advancing the data pointer past each datum used. | PRT-0111 |
| 10.5.4.1 | A-10.5.4.1-02 | semantics | core | Each datum read for an array element must match the type of that element. | PRT-0112 |
| 10.5.4.1 | A-10.5.4.1-03 | semantics | core | A redim resizes the array before values are stored, using the index values as the new bounds; if resizing fails the array keeps its old shape; redims are evaluated after the arrays to their left were filled. | PRT-0113 |
| 10.5.4.1 | A-10.5.4.1-04 | semantics | core | Running out of data in MAT READ behaves exactly as in plain READ, with or without IF MISSING: with the recovery the jump is taken and the array keeps its size. | PRT-0115 |
| 10.5.4.1 | A-10.5.4.1-05 | semantics | core | A numeric datum read for an array that underflows is stored as zero. | PRT-0116 |
| 10.5.4.1 | A-10.5.4.1-06 | semantics | core | MAT READ reports the nonfatal exception 1506 for an underflowing numeric DATA datum, exactly as scalar READ does, after storing zero in that element. | PRT-0150 |
| 10.5.4.1 | A-10.5.4.1-07 | semantics | core | MAT READ assigns its data one by one in row major order, like READ: when a string datum is longer than the length-max of the array (1053) or a nonnumeric datum is read for a numeric array (8101), the elements before the failing one stay assigned and the later ones keep their old values; this holds for one, two and three dimensions, for several arrays in one statement and with IF MISSING. | ARR-0220 |
| 10.5.4.1 | A-10.5.4.1-08 | semantics | core | MAT READ with insufficient data works like READ: the values are assigned one by one and the data pointer advances beyond each datum, so the data that are present are assigned and consumed when exception 8001 occurs (in a WHEN block) or when the missing-recovery (IF MISSING) is taken, for one array, for the array that runs out among several, for a redim and for a string array; the elements not reached keep their old values and the next READ finds no data. | ARR-0230 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-01 | semantics | core | MAT INPUT waits for a valid input-reply, then fills the listed arrays in order, all elements row by row. | PRT-0117 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-02 | semantics | core | In interactive mode MAT INPUT shows the same input-prompt as plain INPUT. | PRT-0118 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-03 | semantics | core | The PROMPT, TIMEOUT and ELAPSED modifiers of MAT INPUT work as in plain INPUT; a datum of the wrong type in the reply is not accepted (warning 8103) and the reply is requested again. | PRT-0119, PRT-0305 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-04 | semantics | core | Each reply datum must match the type of the array element it lands in. | PRT-0120 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-05 | semantics | core | A redim in MAT INPUT resizes the array before assignment, as in MAT READ, and is evaluated after the arrays to its left were filled. | PRT-0121 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-06 | semantics | core | Array input may span several replies: while data are still missing and the reply ends with a comma, the prompt is issued again and another reply is read. | PRT-0122 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-07 | semantics | core | A numeric input datum that underflows is stored as zero. | PRT-0123 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-08 | semantics | core | In MAT INPUT, elements whose data were validated before an 8002, 8103 or 1007 remain assigned (row major order); the exception is raised after them. | PRT-0147, PRT-0148, PRT-0151 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-09 | semantics | core | When a string overflow (1054) interrupts the reply of MAT INPUT and is handled by a WHEN block, the elements already assigned before the failing one stay assigned (row major order, in one, two and three dimensions, for several arrays in one statement and for a variable-length vector) and the later elements keep their old values. Agreed interpretation of 10.5.4.2 (interpretations.yaml). | PRT-0220 |
| 10.5.4.2 | A-10.5.4.2-10 | semantics | core | When the input runs out (end of file, 8011) in the middle of MAT INPUT and the exception is handled by a WHEN block, the data already supplied stay assigned (the arrays completed before and the elements of the current array already validated) and the elements not reached keep their old values, as with INPUT. Agreed interpretation of 10.5.4.2 (interpretations.yaml). | PRT-0241 |
| 10.5.4.3 | A-10.5.4.3-01 | semantics | core | A question-mark vector takes as many data as the reply (or the replies up to the first one not ending in a comma) contains, starting at the vector's current lower bound; afterwards its upper bound is set to the subscript that received the last datum, and the count may not exceed the size declared for the vector. | PRT-0124, PRT-0125 |
| 10.5.4.3 | A-10.5.4.3-02 | semantics | core | Reply data for a question-mark vector must match the type of the vector. | PRT-0126 |
| 10.5.4.4 | A-10.5.4.4-01 | semantics | core | MAT LINE INPUT reads one whole line per element of each string array, storing the lines (without their end-of-lines) row by row; the number of lines read equals the number of elements. | PRT-0127 |
| 10.5.4.4 | A-10.5.4.4-03 | semantics | core | The input modifiers of MAT LINE INPUT work as in plain INPUT. | PRT-0128 |
| 10.5.4.4 | A-10.5.4.4-04 | semantics | core | A redim in MAT LINE INPUT resizes the string array before assignment, as in MAT READ, and is evaluated after the string arrays to its left were filled. | PRT-0129 |
| 10.5.4.4 | A-10.5.4.4-05 | semantics | core | When a string overflow (1054) interrupts a line reply of MAT LINE INPUT and is handled by a WHEN block, the lines already accepted stay assigned to their elements (row major order, in one, two and three dimensions and for several arrays in one statement) and the later elements keep their old values. | PRT-0221 |
| 10.5.4.4 | A-10.5.4.4-06 | semantics | core | When the input runs out (end of file, 8011) in the middle of MAT LINE INPUT and the exception is handled by a WHEN block, the lines already supplied stay assigned to their elements and the elements not reached keep their old values, as with LINE INPUT. Agreed interpretation of 10.5.4.2 (interpretations.yaml). | PRT-0242 |
| 10.5.4.5 | A-10.5.4.5-01 | semantics | core | MAT PRINT outputs every element of every listed array; when the current output line already has characters, an end-of-line comes first. | PRT-0130 |
| 10.5.4.5 | A-10.5.4.5-02 | semantics | core | With a plain array list, a 2-D array prints like its elements listed row by row and joined with the separator after the array name (comma when none), plus an end-of-line after each row when one was not already emitted; a 3-D array prints as a series of such 2-D blocks with an extra end-of-line between blocks; a 1-D array prints like a single row. | PRT-0131 |
| 10.5.4.5 | A-10.5.4.5-03 | semantics | core | Between two arrays of an array-print-list one extra end-of-line is emitted. | PRT-0132 |
| 10.5.4.5 | A-10.5.4.5-04 | semantics | core | With USING, the arrays print exactly as their elements listed array by array in row-major order through the image, with no extra line breaks; a final end-of-line follows all output unless the list ends with a semicolon. | PRT-0133 |
| 10.5.4.5 | A-10.5.4.5-05 | semantics | core | An array-print-statement without USING breaks lines at the margin just as the equivalent print-statement does: a vector of ten numbers printed with a semicolon and a margin of 20 puts six items on the first line and the rest on the next, because an item that does not fit goes whole to the following line. | PRT-0404 |
| 10.5.4.5 | A-10.5.4.5-CL40 | exception | core | When a user exception-handler handles the nonfatal exception 3101 raised by a MAT PRINT of an array with elements never assigned, the statement does not complete: the elements of that array are not printed and the handler receives the exception. | PRT-0409 |
| 10.5.5 | A-10.5.5-EXC | exception | core | In MAT READ, assigning a non-numeric datum to a numeric-array element raises fatal exception 8101 (E-8101); resizing an array past the element count reserved by its original declaration raises fatal exception 5001; a redim whose first bound exceeds the second, or a lone bound below the default lower bound, raises fatal exception 6005. | PRT-0134, PRT-0135, PRT-0136, PRT-0137 |
| 10.5.5 | A-10.5.5-TR80 | exception | core | In MAT INPUT, an exception 8002, 8003, 8102, 8103, 1007 or 1054 in an input-reply that is not the first one asks for that reply again and keeps the data of the earlier replies, whatever the arrays involved: several arrays sharing the replies (the rejected reply starts in the array where it is detected or in an earlier one and crosses into it), a single array, a string array and a variable-length vector; a rejected reply with a final comma does not read the next reply before it is asked again. | PRT-0240 |
| 11 | A-11-01 | semantics | files | The implementation supplies some means of creating, preserving and retrieving files, and the input and output operations on those files behave exactly as this section prescribes. | FIL-0029 |
| 11 | A-11-02 | semantics | files | A device need not accept the minimum record size of 132 characters, but the implementation documents the smallest record size each supported device accepts. | FIL-0030 |
| 11 | A-11-03 | semantics | files | On interactive terminal devices the prompt, timeout and time-inquiry input controls are supported, and the implementation defines which devices count as interactive terminals. | FIL-0031 |
| 11.1 | A-11.1.5-03 | semantics | files | OPEN with ACCESS INPUT of a file that exists opens it and the records can be read. | FIL-0020 |
| 11.1.2 | A-11.1.2-01 | syntax | files | Each file attribute may occur at most once in the attribute list of an OPEN. | FIL-0032, FIL-0212, FIL-0213, FIL-0214 |
| 11.1.2 | A-11.1.2-02 | syntax | files | Each ask attribute name may occur at most once in the item list of an ASK statement. | FIL-0033 |
| 11.1.2 | A-11.1.2-03 | syntax | files | The variables of an ask item must agree in number and type with the value of that ask attribute. | FIL-0034 |
| 11.1.2 | A-11.1.2-TR176 | semantics | files | A channel-expression is a number-sign followed by an index, so a channel number that is not an integer is rounded with INT(X+.5) in OPEN, CLOSE, PRINT, LINE INPUT, ASK, SET and the other file statements: #1.4 and #0.6 are channel 1. The rounded value is then checked against the range of channels: #255.4 is channel 255 and is valid, #255.6 is channel 256 (7001), #0.4 is channel zero (7002) and #-.6 is channel -1 (7001). | FIL-0501, FIL-0502 |
| 11.1.2 | A-ECMA-30 | semantics | files | OPEN with channel and name expressions, CLOSE, ERASE and ERASE REST, and ASK of file attributes including KEY work as written; ASK NUMCHARS is rejected (known deviation). | ECMA-0067, ECMA-0068, ECMA-0069, ECMA-0070, ECMA-0071 |
| 11.1.3 | A-11.1.3-EX | syntax | files | Every OPEN, CLOSE, ERASE and ASK form shown in the examples of section 11.1.3 is accepted. | FIL-0035 |
| 11.1.4 | A-11.1.4-01 | semantics | files | Channel numbers run from zero up to an implementation-defined maximum that is at least 99. | FIL-0036 |
| 11.1.4 | A-11.1.4-02 | semantics | files | When a program starts, every channel except channel zero is inactive, and channel zero is always active. | FIL-0037 |
| 11.1.4 | A-11.1.4-03 | semantics | files | Channel zero sends and receives exactly where the plain INPUT and PRINT statements do, and acts as a sequential, display, outin device with no record-setter and no erase capability. | FIL-0038 |
| 11.1.4 | A-11.1.4-TR124 | semantics | files | In a STREAM INTERNAL file a multi-value WRITE is still a sequence of individual values: after reading some of them ASK POINTER is MIDDLE (not END) and ERASE REST deletes the values at or beyond the pointer while keeping the preceding ones. | FIL-0415, FIL-0416 |
| 11.1.4.1 | A-11.1.4.1-01 | semantics | files | After a successful OPEN the channel is active and the file open; opening a channel that is already active raises an exception, and at least one nonzero channel (two with the enhanced files module) can be active at a time. | FIL-0039 |
| 11.1.4.1 | A-11.1.4.1-02 | semantics | files | After a successful OPEN a true file is accessible according to its attributes, explicit or default; if it cannot be made accessible that way, an exception results. | FIL-0040 |
| 11.1.4.1 | A-11.1.4.1-03 | semantics | files | A true file reopened with the same attributes, collate sequence and arithmetic option, and whose contents were preserved meanwhile, is accessible again with its contents faithfully intact. | FIL-0041 |
| 11.1.4.1 | A-11.1.4.1-04 | semantics | files | The core module accepts and processes sequential display, sequential internal and stream internal files. | FIL-0042 |
| 11.1.4.1 | A-11.1.4.1-05 | semantics | files | The enhanced internal module also accepts and processes relative internal and keyed internal files. | FIL-0043 |
| 11.1.4.1 | A-11.1.4.1-06 | semantics | files | The enhanced native module also accepts and processes sequential native, relative native and keyed native files. | FIL-0044 |
| 11.1.4.1 | A-11.1.4.1-07 | syntax | files | Letters in a string used as a file attribute value match the keyword regardless of case. | FIL-0045 |
| 11.1.4.2 | A-11.1.4.2-01 | semantics | files | With access mode INPUT the file can be read but not changed: READ, SET with pointer items and INPUT are allowed, PRINT, WRITE, REWRITE and DELETE are not. | FIL-0046 |
| 11.1.4.2 | A-11.1.4.2-02 | semantics | files | With access mode OUTPUT new data can be appended but existing data can be neither changed nor read back; the permitted statements are PRINT, SET with pointer control and WRITE, while READ, REWRITE, DELETE and INPUT are rejected. | FIL-0047, FIL-0603 |
| 11.1.4.2 | A-11.1.4.2-03 | semantics | files | ERASE is allowed only on a file whose access mode is OUTIN. | FIL-0048 |
| 11.1.4.2 | A-11.1.4.2-04 | semantics | files | When OPEN omits the access mode, a file that can be read and written gets OUTIN, one that can only be read gets INPUT and one that can only be written gets OUTPUT; channel zero acts as OUTIN. | FIL-0049 |
| 11.1.4.2 | A-11.1.4.2-05 | semantics | files | After OPEN with access mode OUTPUT the file pointer sits at end of file; with any other access mode it sits at the beginning. | FIL-0050, FIL-0604 |
| 11.1.4.3 | A-11.1.4.3-01 | semantics | files | When OPEN omits the organization, it is taken from system information about the file if available, and otherwise the file is opened as SEQUENTIAL; channel zero acts as SEQUENTIAL. | FIL-0051 |
| 11.1.4.4 | A-11.1.4.4-01 | semantics | files | When OPEN omits the record type, it is taken from system information about the file if available, and otherwise the file is opened as DISPLAY; channel zero acts as DISPLAY. | FIL-0052 |
| 11.1.4.5 | A-11.1.4.5-01 | semantics | files | All files consist of variable-length records, and the length of a DISPLAY record is its number of characters. | FIL-0053 |
| 11.1.4.5 | A-11.1.4.5-02 | semantics | files | A record operation on a record longer than the maximum record size set explicitly or by default at OPEN raises an exception. | FIL-0054 |
| 11.1.4.5 | A-11.1.4.5-03 | semantics | files | When OPEN omits the record size, it is taken from system information if available and otherwise the file is opened as VARIABLE; channel zero acts as VARIABLE with no length index. | FIL-0055 |
| 11.1.4.5 | A-11.1.4.5-TR177 | semantics | files | The index of RECSIZE VARIABLE LENGTH is rounded to an integer and only then must be greater than zero: LENGTH .4 evaluates to 0 and gives the exception 7051, while LENGTH .5 evaluates to 1 and is a valid maximum record length (the margin of the file). | FIL-0504 |
| 11.1.4.6 | A-11.1.4.6-01 | semantics | files | The collate sequence of a KEYED file governs every record operation on it and the ERASE of the whole file. | FIL-0056 |
| 11.1.4.6 | A-11.1.4.6-02 | semantics | files | A program unit whose collate sequence differs from the file's can still access a KEYED file; only the logical order of the records may differ, never their contents. | FIL-0057 |
| 11.1.4.6 | A-11.1.4.6-03 | semantics | files | When OPEN omits the collate sequence, it is taken from system information if available, otherwise the sequence in effect for the program unit is used. | FIL-0058, FIL-0209, FIL-0215 |
| 11.1.4.7 | A-11.1.4.7-01 | semantics | files | CLOSE closes the file on the given channel and makes the channel inactive; closing a channel with no file does nothing. | FIL-0059 |
| 11.1.4.7 | A-11.1.4.7-02 | semantics | files | Files opened inside an external procedure or a parallel section are closed when it ends, unless the channel is a formal parameter, and any file still open is closed when the program terminates. | FIL-0060 |
| 11.1.4.7 | A-11.1.4.7-CL39 | semantics | files | On exit from an external SUB, FUNCTION or PICTURE, the files that procedure opened on channels that are not formal parameters are closed, and a partial record left by a PRINT # with a trailing print-separator is completed with an end-of-record; a later PRINT # to that channel gives exception 7004 and a later opening of the file starts a new record. | FIL-0572 |
| 11.1.4.7 | A-11.1.4.7-CL42 | semantics | files | On exit from an external unit, and on program termination, the closing of a RELATIVE DISPLAY file completes the partial record left by a PRINT # with a trailing print-separator, exactly as an explicit CLOSE does, so a later reading by record number finds the record. | FIL-0573 |
| 11.1.4.8 | A-11.1.4.8-01 | semantics | files | ERASE on a true file deletes all or part of its data without changing the file attributes. | FIL-0061 |
| 11.1.4.9 | A-11.1.4.9-01 | semantics | files | ASK assigns to its variables the values of the attributes of the file on the given channel. | FIL-0062 |
| 11.1.4.9 | A-11.1.4.9-02 | semantics | files | ASK on an inactive channel assigns the null string to every string variable and zero to every numeric variable. | FIL-0063 |
| 11.1.4.9 | A-11.1.4.9-03 | syntax | files | The POINTER ask-value is BEGIN, MIDDLE or END, where MIDDLE means neither of the other two and END also covers an empty file. | FIL-0064 |
| 11.1.4.9 | A-11.1.4.9-04 | semantics | files | ASK #n: MARGIN assigns the current margin of a DISPLAY file (MAXNUM when the record may be of arbitrary length, i.e. no RECSIZE LENGTH and no SET #n: MARGIN, or after SET #n: MARGIN MAXNUM), the RECSIZE LENGTH when the file was opened with one, the value set by SET #n: MARGIN otherwise, and zero for a non-DISPLAY file. | FIL-0189 |
| 11.1.4.9 | A-11.1.4.9-05 | semantics | files | In a STREAM INTERNAL file, DATUM reports the type of the next datum after the current pointer: after a partial READ of a multi-datum WRITE the pointer is at the next pending value of that WRITE (§11.4.4 l.8056-8062), so DATUM gives its type (NUMERIC/STRING), and NONE at end of file; SET #n: POINTER BEGIN/END repositions the pointer and DATUM follows it. | FIL-0195 |
| 11.1.4.9 | A-11.1.4.9-TR48 | semantics | files | ASK #n: ZONEWIDTH assigns the current zone width for a DISPLAY file (default 17, or the value of the last SET #n: ZONEWIDTH) and zero for a non-DISPLAY file (Table 5). ASK #n: MARGIN is zero for a non-DISPLAY file as well. | FIL-0207 |
| 11.1.4.9 | A-11.1.4.9-TR48KEY | semantics | files | ASK #n: KEY on a KEYED file assigns the key of the record identified by the pointer, and the null string when the pointer is at end of file (Table 5) — e.g. after an inexact greater-than search (SET #n: KEY > k$) with no greater key, which sets the pointer to end of file (§11.2.4.1); the null string is also assigned for a non-KEYED file. | FIL-0208 |
| 11.1.4.9 | A-11.1.4.9-TR64 | semantics | files | On a KEYED file, after a READ # (with or without a record-setter, exact or inexact) the pointer is at the next file-element, so ASK #n: KEY gives the key of the NEXT record in the key sequence (not the one just read) and the null string once the last record has been read; after SET #n: KEY the pointer is at the record found, and ASK KEY gives its key. | FIL-0219 |
| 11.1.5 | A-11.1.5-01 | exception | files | OPEN with ACCESS INPUT of a file that does not exist raises a 71xx exception (not 7100, which is an unrecognizable attribute), which a handler can intercept and which reports the line of the OPEN. | FIL-0018 |
| 11.1.5 | A-11.1.5-CL05 | exception | files | An OPEN whose NAME evaluates to the empty string, whether given as a literal, a variable or an empty substring, raises an exception in the 71xx range, since access to the file is not possible, and not a code outside the standard ranges. | FIL-0564 |
| 11.1.5 | E-7001 | exception | files | A channel expression outside the range zero to the maximum raises the fatal exception 7001. | FIL-0076, FIL-0569, FIL-0570, FIL-0571 |
| 11.1.5 | E-7002 | exception | files | OPEN, CLOSE or ERASE on channel zero, and any record-setter used with channel zero, raise the nonfatal exception 7002: nothing happens and execution continues. | FIL-0077 |
| 11.1.5 | E-7003 | exception | files | OPEN on a nonzero channel that is already active raises the fatal exception 7003. | FIL-0078 |
| 11.1.5 | E-7004 | exception | files | Any file statement other than OPEN or ASK executed on an inactive channel raises the fatal exception 7004. | FIL-0079 |
| 11.1.5 | E-7050 | exception | files | Reopening a KEYED file with a collate sequence different from an earlier open raises the fatal exception 7050. | FIL-0080 |
| 11.1.5 | E-7051 | exception | files | A LENGTH index not greater than zero in an OPEN raises the fatal exception 7051. | FIL-0081 |
| 11.1.5 | E-7100 | exception | files | A string used as a file attribute in OPEN whose value is not a recognized keyword raises the fatal exception 7100. | FIL-0082, FIL-0563 |
| 11.1.5 | E-71xx | exception | files | When a file cannot be given the access the requested or default attributes demand, a fatal 71xx exception is raised whose exact value and meaning are implementation-defined. | FIL-0083 |
| 11.1.5 | E-7301 | exception | files | ERASE on a file not opened as OUTIN raises the fatal exception 7301 and has no effect on the file. | FIL-0084 |
| 11.2.2 | A-11.2.2-TR155 | syntax | files | The line-number of the io-recovery of the pointer-items of a SET (SET #n: POINTER ..., IF MISSING THEN n; IF THERE THEN n; KEY ..., IF MISSING THEN n) is the line of a control-transfer (8.2.2 prod. 1): it must exist in the program unit (4.2.2) and obeys the same scope rules as GOTO, so from outside it may not name a line inside an if-block branch, select-block case, for-body, do-body, protection-block, exception-handler or the header line of its own external subprogram, nor may it jump between sibling branches or leave an internal routine; jumps within the same branch or to the end-if-line stay valid. | FIL-0492, FIL-0493, FIL-0494, FIL-0495, FIL-0496, FIL-0497, FIL-0498, FIL-0499, FIL-0500 |
| 11.2.2 | A-ECMA-31 | semantics | files | SET # with POINTER BEGIN, RECORD and KEY (with IF MISSING / IF THERE) positions the pointer as written; the channel must be a literal here (known deviation). | ECMA-0072 |
| 11.2.3 | A-11.2.3-EX | syntax | files | Every SET with pointer items form shown in the examples of section 11.2.3 is accepted. | FIL-0065 |
| 11.2.4 | A-11.2.4-01 | semantics | files | A SET statement with pointer items moves the file pointer of the file on the given channel. | FIL-0066 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-01 | semantics | files | NEXT moves the pointer to the next existing record or value at or beyond the current position, skipping empty record areas of a RELATIVE file, and leaves the pointer alone when it already sits at an existing element or at end of file. | FIL-0067 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-02 | semantics | files | On a SEQUENTIAL file with a partial record pending, NEXT emits the end-of-record and leaves the pointer at end of file. | FIL-0068 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-03 | semantics | files | On a KEYED file NEXT leaves the pointer unchanged, so a read after it still returns the record the pointer already designates and a loop of NEXT then READ visits every key in collating order. | FIL-0194 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-04 | semantics | files | When the most recent operation on the channel was a WRITE or PRINT, a subsequent SAME record-setter points at the first file element that the operation created: after two single-value WRITEs on a SEQUENTIAL file, READ #, SAME (or SET # POINTER SAME followed by READ #) reads back the second record; a multi-value WRITE on SEQUENTIAL creates a single record (SAME reads it whole) and on STREAM each value is its own element (SAME reads the first value). | FIL-0204 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-05 | semantics | files | SAME is valid after a MAT WRITE and after a WRITE or MAT WRITE with a template (NATIVE file) on a SEQUENTIAL file, exactly as after a scalar WRITE: it points at the first file element created by that operation, so a read after SET # POINTER SAME returns the values just written and the exception 7204 does not occur. | FIL-0505 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-CL02 | semantics | files | REWRITE, MAT REWRITE and DELETE on a KEYED file set the pointer from the KEY record-setter exactly as the data retrieval statements do: with KEY >= s (not-less) they act on the record whose key equals s or else on the first record whose key is greater, and with KEY > s on the first record whose key is strictly greater; only when no such record exists (pointer at end of file) or an exact search finds no equal key is data-found false and the exception 7305 given with the file unchanged. | FIL-0560 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-G01 | semantics | files | SET # with an exact KEY search on a KEYED file sets the pointer to the record whose key equals the string. | FIL-0177 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-G02 | semantics | files | SET # with an inexact KEY search sets the pointer to the first record with a strictly greater key, and an exact miss leaves data-found false. | FIL-0178 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-TR105 | semantics | files | On a STREAM file, SAME after a READ resets the pointer to the file element the pointer had at the beginning of that READ: after READ #1: A and READ #1: B on a file holding 1, 2, 3, SET #1: POINTER SAME followed by READ #1: C gives C = 2 (not 1), and after three READs a SAME followed by READ gives the third value. | FIL-0385 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-TR114 | semantics | files | On a RELATIVE file, the NEXT record-setter puts the pointer at the next existing record at or beyond the current position: if the pointer is already on an existing record it is unchanged (SET POINTER BEGIN then READ NEXT reads the first record), on an empty area it moves to the next existing record, and at or beyond the last record it stays. | FIL-0406, FIL-0407, FIL-0408, FIL-0409 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-TR123 | semantics | files | On a KEYED file the NEXT record-setter leaves the pointer unchanged wherever it is: after SET POINTER BEGIN a READ NEXT reads the first record and the current key does not change, successive READ NEXT visit every record without skipping any, and NEXT after a READ, after a DELETE or at end of file does not move the pointer. | FIL-0413, FIL-0414 |
| 11.2.4.1 | A-11.2.4.1-TR177 | semantics | files | The index of a RECORD record-setter is evaluated by rounding to an integer and only then compared with one: RECORD .7 is record 1 and RECORD 1.6 is record 2, while RECORD .4 evaluates to 0 and gives the exception 7206. | FIL-0503 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-01 | semantics | files | On a sequential file, WRITE # with an if-there io-recovery takes the recovery action when the pointer identifies an existing record, and leaves the file unchanged. | FIL-0015 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-02 | semantics | files | On a sequential file, PRINT # with an if-there io-recovery takes the recovery action when the pointer identifies an existing record, and leaves the file unchanged. | FIL-0016 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-03 | semantics | files | On a sequential file, an if-there io-recovery is not taken when the pointer is at end of file, so the data is written. | FIL-0017 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-04 | semantics | files | A not-missing-recovery that is not taken because data-found is false is ignored: it does not carry over to a later write, which on an existing record without a recovery raises exception 7308, in relative and keyed files. | FIL-0023 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-05 | semantics | files | After pointer manipulation the data-found condition is set, either true or false. | FIL-0069 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-06 | semantics | files | An io-recovery action that is an EXIT DO or EXIT FOR has its normal effect, and one that is a line number continues execution at that line. | FIL-0070 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-07 | semantics | files | A set-statement with pointer-items takes its io-recovery according to the data-found condition after pointer manipulation: POINTER END leaves the pointer at end of file so IF MISSING is taken (data-found false, case 2), an io-recovery without pointer-control is valid syntax and still has its usual effect with the pointer unchanged, POINTER BEGIN with data present takes IF THERE, and an IF MISSING THEN EXIT FOR action exits the loop on the first iteration. | FIL-0201, FIL-0065 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-08 | semantics | files | On a KEYED file, SET # with an exact KEY search that finds no equal key sets data-found false (case 1) so IF MISSING is taken, an exact hit or an inexact search that lands on a record sets data-found true so IF THERE is taken, and an inexact search past the last key leaves the pointer at end of file (case 2) so IF MISSING is taken. | FIL-0202 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-09 | semantics | files | On a RELATIVE file, SET # with RECORD pointing to an empty record-area or POINTER END (beyond the last existing record) sets data-found false so IF MISSING is taken, and RECORD pointing to an occupied area sets data-found true so IF MISSING is not taken. | FIL-0203 |
| 11.2.4.2 | A-11.2.4.2-TR115 | semantics | files | The io-recovery of a file statement applies only to that statement: a missing-recovery or there-recovery that did not fire is not applied to later statements of the channel that carry none (a SET, or a READ of a missing record, which is then 7305). | FIL-0410, FIL-0411, FIL-0412 |
| 11.2.5 | A-11.2.5-CL07 | exception | files | A record-setter used with channel zero gives the nonfatal exception 7002 in every statement that accepts one, INPUT and LINE INPUT included. With an active handler of the program the exception is delivered to the handler, EXTYPE is 7002 and the statement reads nothing; with no handler it is reported as a warning, execution continues and the statement is carried out with the record-setter ignored. | FIL-0566 |
| 11.2.5 | E-7202 | exception | files | The RECORD record-setter on a file whose organization is not RELATIVE raises the fatal exception 7202 and leaves the pointer unchanged. | FIL-0071 |
| 11.2.5 | E-7203 | exception | files | The KEY record-setter on a file whose organization is not KEYED raises the fatal exception 7203 and leaves the pointer unchanged. | FIL-0072 |
| 11.2.5 | E-7204 | exception | files | SAME raises the fatal exception 7204 when the last operation on the channel was a DELETE, when it raised an exception before moving the pointer, or when no record operation has run on the channel since the OPEN. | FIL-0073 |
| 11.2.5 | E-7206 | exception | files | A RECORD index that rounds to an integer below one raises the fatal exception 7206. | FIL-0074 |
| 11.2.5 | E-7207 | exception | files | An exact key search whose key expression is the null string raises the fatal exception 7207. | FIL-0075 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-01 | syntax | files | PRINT # accepts an if-there io-recovery in its print control; when no record exists at the pointer nothing is taken and the data is written. | FIL-0001 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-02 | semantics | files | PRINT # with an if-there io-recovery takes the recovery action when a record exists at the pointer, and leaves the file unchanged. | FIL-0002 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-03 | syntax | files | The recovery action of an if-there in PRINT # may be EXIT DO. | FIL-0003 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-04 | semantics | files | A data creation statement on a sequential file whose pointer is at end of file appends a record and raises no exception. | FIL-0028 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-05 | syntax | files | An image in the print control of PRINT # requires an output list, never a print list. | FIL-0113 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-06 | syntax | files | The line number of a template identifier must point to a TEMPLATE statement of the same program unit. | FIL-0114 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-07 | syntax | files | The integer of a fixed field count must be greater than zero, and of the integer-size and fraction-size of a fixed-point size at least one must be greater than zero. | FIL-0115 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-08 | syntax | files | A string field size must be greater than zero. | FIL-0116 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-09 | syntax | files | The record setter of a write control must not use an inexact key search: WRITE #1, KEY > k$ and KEY >= k$ (also in MAT WRITE) is rejected when the program is loaded, before any statement runs, and not by the run-time exception 7314 (which remains for a write to a KEYED file with no exact search at all). | FIL-0117, FIL-0218 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-10 | syntax | files | Each item of a print, write, input, read, rewrite or delete control may appear at most once in that control. | FIL-0118 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-11 | syntax | files | An image (USING) in the print-control of MAT PRINT # requires an array output list (comma-separated array names with at most one final semicolon), never an array print list: a mid-list semicolon or a trailing comma is rejected at load. | FIL-0185, FIL-0186, FIL-0187 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-12 | syntax | files | A template-statement may declare a NUMERIC*E field (numeric-field-size = fixed-point-size / E), and WITH <line-number> can use that template; only E (not another identifier) is accepted after NUMERIC*. | FIL-0188, ECMA-0087 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-13 | syntax | files | The output-list of PRINT # USING is expression (comma expression)* with an optional final semicolon: a trailing comma is rejected at load. | FIL-0192 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-TR106 | syntax | files | A WITH <line> template-identifier in WRITE, REWRITE, READ, MAT WRITE, MAT READ or MAT REWRITE whose line is not a TEMPLATE statement of the same program unit (a plain statement, a missing line, or a TEMPLATE of another unit) is rejected before the program runs, independently of the order of the lines. | FIL-0388, FIL-0386, FIL-0387 |
| 11.3.2 | A-11.3.2-TR113 | syntax | files | Two record-setters, even different ones (BEGIN and END, NEXT and KEY, SAME and RECORD), in the control of one PRINT #, INPUT #, READ #, WRITE #, REWRITE # or DELETE # make the program invalid and it is rejected before it runs. | FIL-0400, FIL-0401, FIL-0402, FIL-0403, FIL-0404, FIL-0405 |
| 11.3.2 | A-ECMA-32 | semantics | files | PRINT # with record controls and USING an IMAGE, MAT PRINT with SAME and IF THERE, SET # MARGIN, WRITE with RECORD and WITH a TEMPLATE, MAT WRITE with KEY, and TEMPLATE declarations work as written; MAT WRITE of a string array whose elements were never assigned writes null strings and warns 3102. | ECMA-0073, ECMA-0074, ECMA-0075, ECMA-0076, ECMA-0077, ECMA-0078, ECMA-0087, ECMA-0088 |
| 11.3.2 | A-ECMA-errata-01 | semantics | files | A KEY record-setter is not allowed inside a PRINT # print-control (the ECMA appendix admits it, the body of 11.3.2 and the ANSI do not); this interpreter rejects it. | ECMA-0105 |
| 11.3.3 | A-11.3.3-EX | syntax | files | Every PRINT, MAT PRINT, WRITE, MAT WRITE, SET MARGIN and TEMPLATE form shown in the examples of section 11.3.3 is accepted. | FIL-0119 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-01 | semantics | files | In a STREAM INTERNAL file, a WRITE # without record-setter after a partial READ # (pointer at a pending value of the same WRITE) leaves the pointer unchanged (§11.2.4.1) with data-found true, so without a not-missing-recovery it raises the fatal exception 7308 and neither the pointer nor the file change; after SET #n: POINTER END the WRITE creates the element at end of file and it reads back. | FIL-0196 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-02 | semantics | files | In a RELATIVE file, a WRITE # that creates a record leaves the file pointer at the next file-element beyond the one created, also when a RECORD record-setter was present: after WRITE #1, RECORD n the pointer is at record-area n+1 (end of file if that is beyond the last existing record), so ASK RECORD/POINTER report it, a following READ # without record-setter finds the next record-area (missing-recovery if empty), and a following WRITE # without record-setter creates the next record (7308 only when the pointer identifies an existing record). | FIL-0197, FIL-0198 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-03 | semantics | files | In a KEYED file, a WRITE # that creates a record leaves the file pointer at the next file-element beyond the one created, that is the next key in the key sequence (also when the new key is inserted between existing ones) or end of file when none follows: ASK KEY then gives that next key (the null string at end of file), a following READ # without record-setter reads the next record, and at end of file it takes the missing-recovery. | FIL-0216 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR48 | semantics | files | In a DISPLAY file, the effective margin (RECSIZE LENGTH at open, or the last SET #n: MARGIN) cuts an overlength print-item mid-item: during the generation of the item, each character that would appear beyond the margin is preceded by an end-of-record and the columnar position resets to one (§10.3.4.4), exactly as end-of-line does on channel zero; a whole item that does not fit is preceded by an end-of-record when the columnar position is greater than one. | FIL-0205, FIL-0206 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR67 | semantics | files | When a data creation statement (WRITE) finds the file-element already present on a RELATIVE or KEYED file, the pointer stays at that existing element, both when a not-missing-recovery (IF THERE) takes the io-recovery-action and when exception 7308 results: after WRITE #n, KEY k$ (or RECORD r) on an existing element, ASK KEY / ASK RECORD give that element and a READ # without record-setter reads it; the file is not changed. | FIL-0220, FIL-0313, FIL-0330 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR71 | semantics | files | On a SEQUENTIAL file, an exception during a WRITE # or PRINT # (in the first, a middle or the last item) never adds a partial file-element: the record that statement was building is not added, so the next statement starts a new record; records already completed before the exception (and a partial record left by an earlier statement with a trailing separator) remain. | FIL-0260, FIL-0261 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR72 | semantics | files | When a third-phase exception (8301, a record larger than the RECSIZE) prevents WRITE or MAT WRITE from creating any file-element on a RELATIVE or KEYED file, the pointer stays where the second phase put it: in a KEYED file at the first key greater than the given one (or at end of file, where ASK KEY gives the null string) and in a RELATIVE file at the record area named by RECORD; no record is created. | FIL-0271 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR81A | semantics | files | When a TEMPLATE exception of the third phase (8252, 8254, 8255 or 8256) prevents WRITE from creating any file-element on a RELATIVE or KEYED file with RECTYPE NATIVE, the pointer stays where the second phase put it: at the record area named by RECORD in a RELATIVE file and at the first key greater than the given one in a KEYED file; no record is created and the next correct WRITE works. | FIL-0290 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR81B | semantics | files | After a handled exception 8301 (record larger than RECSIZE) on a WRITE, MAT WRITE, REWRITE or MAT REWRITE of a RELATIVE or KEYED file (RECTYPE INTERNAL or DISPLAY), nothing of the aborted statement is left on the channel: a following WRITE, REWRITE or MAT REWRITE of a record that fits works and stores only its own data. | FIL-0292 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR83A | semantics | files | On RELATIVE and KEYED files (INTERNAL, NATIVE and DISPLAY), a WRITE or REWRITE stopped by exception 7308 or by an exception while evaluating an operand (the first, a middle one or the last) adds or changes no file-element and leaves no values behind: the next correct WRITE or REWRITE of the channel stores exactly its own values, and the record that failed does not exist (WRITE) or is unchanged (REWRITE). | FIL-0310, FIL-0311, FIL-0312 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR83B | semantics | files | A WRITE with IF THERE (or a REWRITE with IF MISSING) takes the io-recovery-action when data-found is true (false for REWRITE) whatever the number of values: on a RELATIVE INTERNAL file the recovery was lost after the first value; the file is not changed and the next statement of the channel works. | FIL-0313 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR87A | semantics | files | A data creation statement (WRITE, PRINT #) evaluates its operands only in phase 3, after phase 2 has decided that no record exists: when the record is found and the statement carries an IF THERE clause its recovery action is taken without evaluating any operand, so an operand that raises an exception or a function with side effects is not executed; the same holds for a REWRITE with IF MISSING when the record does not exist. When data-found is false the operands are evaluated once, in order. | FIL-0340 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR87B | semantics | files | The exceptions of phases 1 and 2 of a WRITE or PRINT # come before the evaluation of the operands: a WRITE on a file opened INPUT is 7302 (also when it carries IF THERE) and a data creation on an existing record without recovery is 7308, whatever the operands are, and in both cases no operand is evaluated and the file does not change. | FIL-0341 |
| 11.3.4 | A-11.3.4-TR87C | semantics | files | The io-recovery-action declared by a WRITE or REWRITE is taken or ignored by that statement only: when the statement stops with an exception (in an operand of phase 3, with 7302 in phase 1, or with 8301 in MAT WRITE) a later statement on the channel does not take the old recovery, so a WRITE on an existing record gives 7308, a READ of a missing record gives 7305 and a SET that finds a record continues normally. | FIL-0343 |
| 11.3.4.1 | A-11.3.4.1-01 | semantics | files | One PRINT # statement on a DISPLAY file creates exactly one record, and no further record follows it. | FIL-0014 |
| 11.3.4.1 | A-11.3.4.1-02 | semantics | files | A PRINT # USING on a DISPLAY file creates one record for each pass of the format-string (an end-of-record replaces each end-of-line), and no further record follows the last one. | FIL-0021, FIL-0191 |
| 11.3.4.1 | A-11.3.4.1-03 | semantics | files | A PRINT # statement with no print items creates a record of zero characters, in sequential and in relative DISPLAY files. | FIL-0022 |
| 11.3.4.1 | A-11.3.4.1-04 | semantics | files | A PRINT # statement whose print-list ends with a print-separator (semicolon or comma) does not end the record: a following print-statement on the same channel continues it, and a print-statement with no items completes it, in sequential and relative DISPLAY files. | FIL-0025 |
| 11.3.4.1 | A-11.3.4.1-05 | semantics | files | A partial record left by a PRINT # (print-list ending with a print-separator) is completed with an end-of-record when the next operation of the channel is anything other than a PRINT # with an absent record-setter, such as CLOSE or MAT PRINT #, so the partial record is not lost in a relative DISPLAY file. | FIL-0190 |
| 11.3.4.1 | A-11.3.4.1-06 | semantics | files | In a SEQUENTIAL DISPLAY file, a partial record left by PRINT # (trailing print-separator) is completed with an end-of-record before any other record operation of the channel that is not a PRINT # with an absent record-setter — e.g. WRITE # starts a new record (two records), as does SET #n: POINTER NEXT — while a SET with only ZONEWIDTH/MARGIN or an ASK does not complete it: the partial survives and the new value applies when it is later completed (11.3.4.4 l.7626-7628, 11.3.4.3 l.7608-7609). | FIL-0200 |
| 11.3.4.1 | A-11.3.4.1-CL33 | semantics | files | When a SEQUENTIAL DISPLAY channel is closed, or the program terminates with the channel still open, while a partial record left by a PRINT # with a trailing print-separator is pending, the partial record is completed with an end-of-record, so a later opening of the file starts a new record instead of continuing the old one. | FIL-0568 |
| 11.3.4.1 | A-11.3.4.1-TR96 | semantics | files | A tab-call in a PRINT # on a DISPLAY file acts as in 10.3.4.3 on the record being built: the argument is rounded to n, n above the margin of the channel is reduced to MOD(n-1,m)+1, spaces are generated up to column n when the current column is not past it, otherwise an end-of-record and n-1 spaces; the column carries over a partial record of a previous PRINT #, and an index below one is the nonfatal exception 4005 (supply 1 and continue). | FIL-0384 |
| 11.3.4.2 | A-11.3.4.2-01 | semantics | files | MAT PRINT # on a DISPLAY file writes the elements of the array as a record of the file, in place of a line. | FIL-0012 |
| 11.3.4.2 | A-11.3.4.2-02 | semantics | files | MAT PRINT # with an if-there io-recovery takes the recovery action when a record exists at the pointer, and leaves the file unchanged. | FIL-0013 |
| 11.3.4.2 | A-11.3.4.2-03 | semantics | files | An array-print-statement whose output list ends with a semicolon leaves a partial record in a DISPLAY file; a following print-statement on the same channel completes that record, in sequential and relative files. | FIL-0024 |
| 11.3.4.2 | A-11.3.4.2-04 | semantics | files | An array print whose output list ends in a separator may leave a partial record that a later print on the same channel completes, and the effective margin governs that completion. | FIL-0120 |
| 11.3.4.3 | A-11.3.4.3-01 | semantics | files | When RECSIZE gives no LENGTH, the effective margin defaults to a length of at least the default zone width. | FIL-0121 |
| 11.3.4.3 | A-11.3.4.3-02 | semantics | files | A margin of MAXNUM lets a record grow without limit, and a margin index below the current zonewidth (so MARGIN 0) raises exception 4006. | FIL-0122 |
| 11.3.4.4 | A-11.3.4.4-01 | semantics | files | On OPEN the zone width of a DISPLAY file takes an implementation-defined default of at least d+e+6 characters. | FIL-0123 |
| 11.3.4.4 | A-11.3.4.4-02 | semantics | files | In a SET ZONEWIDTH the index must evaluate above zero, and the new zone width also applies when a pending partial record is later completed. | FIL-0124 |
| 11.3.4.6 | A-11.3.4.6-01 | semantics | files | PRINT to channel zero goes where plain PRINT goes, file exceptions use the recovery rules of section 10 there, and SET MARGIN or ZONEWIDTH on channel zero acts as if no channel were given. | FIL-0125 |
| 11.3.4.6 | A-11.3.4.6-TR96 | semantics | files | PRINT #0 with a tab-call behaves as PRINT without a channel: TAB positions the column of the console line, a column already past n starts a new line, and an index below one is 4005. | PRT-0304 |
| 11.3.4.8 | A-11.3.4.8-01 | semantics | files | Writing to a KEYED file always requires an exact key search in the record setter. | FIL-0126 |
| 11.3.4.11 | A-11.3.4.11-01 | syntax | files | Writing to a NATIVE file always needs a TEMPLATE, and no other record type may use one. | FIL-0127 |
| 11.3.4.11 | A-11.3.4.11-02 | syntax | files | A template identifier given as a string expression must evaluate to a syntactically correct template element list, and it is evaluated before the output operands. | FIL-0128 |
| 11.3.4.11 | A-11.3.4.11-03 | semantics | files | A native write may not have more expressions than template specifiers; surplus specifiers are ignored. | FIL-0129 |
| 11.3.4.11 | A-11.3.4.11-04 | semantics | files | A SKIP inside a field count makes the governed specifiers produce skipped fields (zeros for numeric, spaces for string) instead of consuming operands. | FIL-0130 |
| 11.3.4.11 | A-11.3.4.11-CL06 | exception | files | In a template, a NUMERIC field whose integer-size is omitted is treated as having integer-size zero: a value that still has a nonzero integer part after rounding to the fraction-size has no available position to the left of the point and gives exception 8255, while a value below one in magnitude is stored and read back, and digits beyond the fraction-size are rounded (possibly to zero). | FIL-0565 |
| 11.3.4.12 | A-11.3.4.12-01 | semantics | files | With a fixed field count, the number and types of the specifiers must match the array elements, as with a plain WRITE or READ. | FIL-0131 |
| 11.3.4.12 | A-11.3.4.12-02 | semantics | files | An array uses either a variable field count or fixed field counts in its template, never both; a variable count that meets the array after a fixed count raises 8253. | FIL-0132 |
| 11.3.5 | E-4006 | exception | files | A SET MARGIN whose index is below the current zone width of the file raises the fatal exception 4006. | FIL-0096 |
| 11.3.5 | E-4007 | exception | files | A SET ZONEWIDTH whose index is below one or above the current margin of the file raises the fatal exception 4007. | FIL-0097 |
| 11.3.5 | E-7312 | exception | files | SET MARGIN or SET ZONEWIDTH on a file not opened as DISPLAY raises the fatal exception 7312. | FIL-0088, FIL-0561 |
| 11.3.5 | E-7313 | exception | files | SET MARGIN or SET ZONEWIDTH on a file opened as INPUT raises the fatal exception 7313. | FIL-0089, FIL-0562 |
| 11.3.5.1 | E-7302 | exception | files | A data creation statement on a file opened as INPUT raises the fatal exception 7302. | FIL-0085 |
| 11.3.5.1 | E-7314 | exception | files | A WRITE or MAT WRITE to a KEYED file whose record setter has no exact search raises the fatal exception 7314. | FIL-0090 |
| 11.3.5.1 | E-7315 | exception | files | Using a template identifier with a file whose record type is DISPLAY or INTERNAL raises the fatal exception 7315. | FIL-0091 |
| 11.3.5.1 | E-7316 | exception | files | Accessing a NATIVE file with a WRITE, READ, REWRITE or DELETE that has no template identifier raises the fatal exception 7316. | FIL-0092 |
| 11.3.5.1 | E-7317 | exception | files | PRINT or MAT PRINT on a file opened as INTERNAL or NATIVE raises the fatal exception 7317. | FIL-0093 |
| 11.3.5.1 | E-8251 | exception | files | A template identifier whose string expression is not a syntactically correct template element list raises the fatal exception 8251. | FIL-0104 |
| 11.3.5.2 | E-7308 | exception | files | A data creation statement on a sequential file whose pointer identifies an existing record, with no not-missing-recovery, raises the fatal exception 7308 and leaves the pointer and the file unchanged. | FIL-0026, FIL-0027 |
| 11.3.5.3 | A-11.3.5.3-TR81A | exception | files | In a SEQUENTIAL file with RECTYPE INTERNAL, WRITE or MAT WRITE of a record larger than the RECSIZE gives exception 8301 and adds nothing to the file, so the records written correctly can be read back without exception 8302. | FIL-0291 |

| 11.4.4.6 | A-11.4.4.6-02 | semantics | files | In INPUT #0 and MAT INPUT #0 an exception 8102, 8103, 8002, 8003, 1007 or 1054 in a reply that is not the first (a continuation after a final comma) asks for the current input-reply again, as INPUT and MAT INPUT do, and keeps the data accepted in the earlier replies; an exception in the first reply restarts the statement. | FIL-0280 |
| 11.4.4.6 | A-11.4.4.6-03 | semantics | files | LINE INPUT #0 and MAT LINE INPUT #0 check the length-max of the string variable like LINE INPUT: a line that does not fit is exception 1054 and the current line-input-reply is asked again (the first variable restarts the statement, later variables and later array elements ask only their own line). | FIL-0281 |
| 11.4.4.6 | A-11.4.4.6-TR84 | semantics | files | INPUT #0 and LINE INPUT #0 into an array element, a substring, a substring of an element, an element of a formal array or a string parameter passed by reference check the length-max of the target like INPUT and LINE INPUT: a reply that does not fit is exception 1054 (nonfatal) and the current reply is asked again, not the fatal 1105 of files. | FIL-0320 |
| 11.4.4.8 | A-11.4.4.8-01 | semantics | files | When end of file arrives while a READ of a STREAM file still has variables to fill, the unfilled ones keep their old values, the pointer rests at end of file and the exception 8011 results. | FIL-0141 |
| 11.4.4.8 | A-11.4.4.8-FI13 | semantics | files | In a SEQUENTIAL file with native records each record operation handles exactly one record: after a read the pointer is at the next record, and SKIP REST ignores the rest of the record. | FIL-0574 |
| 11.4.4.9 | A-11.4.4.9-01 | semantics | files | String data is retrieved from a DISPLAY record the way section 10 reads input replies. | FIL-0142 |
| 11.4.4.9 | A-11.4.4.9-02 | semantics | files | Numeric data from a DISPLAY record is read with the accuracy of assigning a numeric constant to a numeric variable. | FIL-0143 |
| 11.4.4.10 | A-11.4.4.10-01 | semantics | files | Values of an INTERNAL element must be fetched into a variable of the same type, otherwise an exception results. | FIL-0144 |
| 11.4.4.10 | A-11.4.4.10-02 | semantics | files | String values retrieved from an INTERNAL file keep their length and content, and numeric values are preserved within the precision limits of the arithmetic option in effect. | FIL-0145 |
| 11.4.4.11 | A-11.4.4.11-01 | syntax | files | Reading a NATIVE record always needs a TEMPLATE, and no other record type may use one. | FIL-0146 |
| 11.4.4.11 | A-11.4.4.11-02 | semantics | files | A native read needs at least as many specifiers as variables; surplus specifiers are ignored. | FIL-0147 |
| 11.4.4.11 | A-11.4.4.11-03 | semantics | files | All field specifiers of a native record must be compatible with those that created the record, otherwise the results are implementation-defined. | FIL-0148 |
| 11.4.4.11 | A-11.4.4.11-04 | syntax | files | Compatibility of specifiers means both string with equal field sizes, both numeric with size E, or both numeric with equal integer and fraction sizes. | FIL-0149 |
