| 15.2.2 | A-15.2.2-03 | syntax | fixed | A fixed-point-type on an internal function line or DEF statement, and a numeric-fixed-parameter, may be used only when the program unit has selected ARITHMETIC FIXED. | FIX-0028, FIX-0029 |
| 15.2.2 | A-15.2.2-04 | syntax | fixed | If a function type declares a fixed defined function, the fixed-point sizes stated, whether explicit or by default, in the declaration and in the matching definition must agree. | FIX-0030 |
| 15.2.2 | A-ECMA-41 | syntax | fixed | Fixed-decimal sizes on arrays and function signatures (A()*8.2, DEF F*10.3(...)) are rejected at load time (known deviation). | ECMA-0103, ECMA-0104 |
| 15.2.3 | A-15.2.3-EX | syntax | fixed | Every parameter and function form shown in the examples of section 15.2.3, fixed formal arrays, fixed defined functions and external functions, is accepted and behaves as written. | FIX-0031 |
| 15.2.4 | A-15.2.4-01 | semantics | fixed | Under ARITHMETIC FIXED, numeric procedure parameters, function parameters and defined functions hold fixed-point decimal values; one whose fixed-point-size is not written takes the default of the ARITHMETIC FIXED option, and a formal array's size applies to each element. | FIX-0032 |
| 15.2.4 | A-15.2.4-02 | semantics | fixed | Arguments of a function reference are bound to the function parameters as in 9.1, except that when the argument's fixed-point-size differs from the parameter's the fixed-point assignment rules of 15.1.4 are used. | FIX-0033 |
| 15.2.4 | A-15.2.4-03 | semantics | fixed | Arguments of a CALL are associated with the subprogram parameters as in 9.2, except that a numeric-expression argument, other than a plain variable, whose fixed-point-size differs from the parameter's is converted using the 15.1.4 assignment rules. | FIX-0034 |

### Agreed interpretations

Readings adopted by this implementation where the standard admits more than one reading or leaves the choice to the project:

| Clause | Topic | Reading adopted | Standard lines |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.4.2 | Function and variable with the same name | A LET A outside the definition of function A is a homonymous variable and enters into conflict; only the function-let inside its own function-def is legal. | l.1458-1466 |
| 4.4.4 | PRINT EXTEXT$ without parentheses | EXTEXT$ is not among the reserved names, and 4.4.4 allows a program to use the name of a supplied function as an ordinary identifier, so PRINT EXTEXT$ without an argument list is a reference to a string variable of that name, not a call to the supplied function. | l.1513-1519 |
| 5.4.4 | ROUND with one argument | ROUND(X) is rejected: the standard defines only ROUND(X,N). | l.1900-1902, l.2015-2017 |
| 5.4.4 | MAX and MIN with a number of arguments other than two | MAX(X,Y) and MIN(X,Y) take exactly two numeric arguments; a call with one, three or more arguments (MAX(1, 2, 3), MIN(5)) is an argument-count mismatch that 5.3.2 requires to agree with the description, and is reported before the program runs (like MOD(5) or ABS(1, 2)). An n-ary MAX or MIN would be an enhancement that the project does not document (2.2 item 9, 2.3 l.580-584). Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-03. | l.1990-1994, l.1775-1777, l.580-584 |
| 5.6.4 | ROUND and binary precision | ROUND is computed in exact decimal over the shortest decimal representation of X; under OPTION ARITHMETIC NATIVE the precision is implementation-defined (section 5, D-5.6-3). | l.2236 |
| 5.6.4 | Trigonometric functions with OPTION ANGLE DEGREES at multiples of 90 degrees | With degrees the argument is exact and the range reduction loses nothing, so the exactness rule applies: when the true result can be written with m+1 significant digits the computed result is exact (SIN(180)=0, COS(90)=0, SIN(90)=1); at the poles (TAN(90), SEC(90), COT(0), CSC(0)) the result is mathematical infinity and exception 1003 is raised. The -2*PI..2*PI limit of 5.4.4 only bounds the loss of range reductions, which is nil in degrees. | l.2253-2262, l.2084-2085, l.2058-2065 |
| 6.4.4 | USING$ with a string as its second argument | USING$(format, value) accepts a string value as well as a number: 6.4.4 describes the numeric form, and 10.4.4.4 (the string-item of a using-list) admits a string, so USING$("##", "a") is valid and yields the string formatted by the string-item rules rather than being rejected at load. Confirmed by the project owner 2026-11-03. | l.2729, 10.4.4.4 |
| 6.4.4 | CHR$ with an argument from 128 to 255 under the STANDARD character set | CHR$(M) for M from 128 to 255 does not raise 4002: the standard leaves the additional other-characters at ordinal positions greater than 127 to the implementation, and the interpreter declares a character set of 256 characters (D-4.1-1), so M is valid up to 255 and CHR$(256) or a negative M still raises 4002; ORD(CHR$(M)) returns M. Confirmed by the project owner 2026-11-04. | l.2609-2611, l.12766-12768 |
| 7.1.2 | Array not declared but redimensioned by a MAT statement | Until it is rejected with its own diagnostic, the redimension list fixes the dimensions of the undeclared array. | l.2997-3002 |
| 7.1.4 | Rounding of N in SIZE/LBOUND/UBOUND | "The value of N is rounded to the nearest integer" is implemented as INT(N+0.5): exact halves round up. | l.3070-3072, l.3082-3084 |
| 7.2.4 | Bounds fixed by a redim-bounds on the destination of a MAT assignment | 7.2.4.3 l.3258-3263 makes the indices of a redim-bounds the lower and upper bounds of the array-value; the destination array is resized as 7.2.4.1 l.3210-3214 orders, so it keeps its old lower bound (new upper = old lower + new size - 1). DIM A(5,5) + MAT A = ZER(0 TO 1, 2 TO 3) leaves A 1..2, 1..2. A single index (ZER(3)) keeps the current default lower bound. MAT READ with a redim is the exception: it fixes both bounds of the destination (10.5.4.1 l.5948-5953). | l.3258-3263, l.3210-3214 |
| 7.3.5 | String overflow when a string-array expression is assigned to an array with a smaller length-max | The overflow of the length-max of the receiving array is reported as 1106, raised by the assignment (l.3468). 1052 (l.3465) is raised by evaluating the expression when an element of the result would exceed the maximum string length of the implementation, 1E9 characters (D-6.2-2): the MAT concatenation raises it before building the element. | l.3465, l.3468 |
| 9.1.2 | Formal parameter homonymous with a function name | It is not treated as a conflict: the standard regulates only its unicity within the parameter list. | l.4266-4268 |
| 9.1.2 | "Same program-unit" in DECLARE EXTERNAL FUNCTION | Read strictly: a DECLARE EXTERNAL FUNCTION in the main program does not cover another external unit; each unit needs its own declaration before the first reference. | l.4201-4205 |
| 9.2.2 | CALL of an internal SUB placed before the SUB definition and its DECLARE SUB | Accepted: 9.2.6 lets an implementation make the internal-sub-type optional even when the definition follows the call. Functions and external subprograms keep the rule that the definition or declaration comes first. | l.4528-4532, l.4771-4774 |
| 9.2.2 | DECLARE INTERNAL SUB in the example of 9.2.6 | Rejected as a syntax error: the syntax of 9.2.2 is internal-sub-type = SUB sub-list, and ECMA-116 has the same production, so the word INTERNAL in the example of 9.2.6 (100 DECLARE INTERNAL SUB S) is an erratum of the example; DECLARE SUB S runs it as written. | l.4497-4499, l.4819 |
| 9.3.6 | Catching 4301, 4302 and 4303 of CHAIN | They are fatal and are not promised to a WHEN handler of the chained-from program: the text lets the chained-from program, the chained-to program or a system program report them. The suite tests them as FATAL. | l.4929-4932 |
| 10.2.2 | "At most one" of each input modifier | "At most one prompt-specifier, one timeout-expression and one time-inquiry" is read per keyword: two occurrences of the same modifier are the same item and are rejected at load, whatever their expressions; different modifiers may still be combined in any sequence. | l.5122-5124 |
| 10.2.4.2 | Assignment before the count/type exceptions of INPUT | "The assignment ... shall take place as soon as an item of data ... has been validated" also holds when a later datum or the reply count fails (8002/8003/8102/8103/1007): every datum already validated stays assigned, and with excess data the 8003 is deferred until the last variable has been assigned, because the count of data is not a property of any single datum. | l.5181-5183, l.5203-5205 |
| 10.3.2 | "A given ask-io-item" means the keyword | Two occurrences of the same ask-io-item (e.g. two MARGIN items with different variables) count as the same item and are rejected at load: the item is identified by its keyword, not by its arguments. | l.5325 |
| 10.3.4.1 | Implicit point only for values that are exactly integers | The implicit-point rule applies to the value of the expression, not to its rounded representation: a non-integer value is one of "all other values" and prints with an explicit period even when rounding to d = 8 digits leaves the fraction empty (2.9999999999 prints as 3., 12345678.9 as 12345679., and so does STR$). A value whose rounded form needs more than d digits uses the scaled form (99999999.6 prints as 1.E+8). | l.5375-5377, l.5379, l.5388-5389, 6.4.4 l.2702-2705 |
| 10.4.4.1 | Stray format-item characters in a PRINT USING format-string | A stray comma, minus sign, plus sign or dollar sign left after a format-item, and an e-format with one or two circumflex accents, make the format-string invalid (8201, fatal): production 8 of 10.4.2 does not admit those characters as a literal-item, so 10.4.4.1 cannot treat them as literals. Characters that are neither literal-items nor format-item characters, such as & or [, also raise 8201. The 10.4.3 example has no stray period after its last format-item: the printed page (p. 123) reads "<$$$$.## $$$$.###^^^^^". Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-07. | l.5587-5594, l.5660, l.5679-5692, l.5831-5832 |
| 10.4.4.3 | PRINT USING: comma after leading percent-sign fill | Leading zeros generated by a percent-sign digit-place count as generated digits, so a comma to their right is inserted (PRINT USING "%,%%%": 12 gives 0,012). Only asterisk and number-sign digit-places substitute the comma by their fill character when no digit precedes it. Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-03. | l.5735-5741, l.5760-5765 |
| 10.5.4.2 | Underflow datum in MAT INPUT | A numeric datum that underflows is stored as zero and the elements already read stay assigned; the 1507 warning (numeric input underflow) is raised after the whole array has been stored, not before assigning anything. | l.6005, l.5071-5072 |
| 10.5.4.2 | MAT INPUT: elements already assigned when a nonfatal exception such as 1054 interrupts the reply | The rule of 10.2.4.2 for INPUT applies: the elements assigned before the exception stay assigned (MAT INPUT D$ with D$(3)*2 and the reply d,abc,e leaves D$(1) = d when 1054 is handled). Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-03. | l.5180-5184 |
| 11.1.2 | Duplicate ask-attribute-name and ASK variables per Table 5 | "A given ask-attribute-name shall appear at most once" is read per keyword; the variables of an ask-item must agree in number and type with Table 5 and each variable of the item receives its own value (RECSIZE A$ N: A$ gets the record-size word, N the maximum record length). | l.6543, l.6546, l.7017 |
| 11.2.5 | PRINT #0, NEXT/SAME/...: record-setter on channel 0 | Warning 7002 is raised and only the record-setter is ignored; the PRINT itself is performed (reading A, confirmed by the project owner 2026-11-03). | l.7303-7304, l.6592-6594 |
| 11.3.2 | Duplicate control items of a file statement | "A given print/write/input/read/rewrite/delete-control-item shall appear at most once" is read per keyword: two IF THERE THEN items with different line numbers are the same item and are rejected at load. | l.7471, l.7474, l.7993, l.7996, l.8504, l.8507 |
| 11.3.2 | "integer-size or fraction-size" means at least one | In a fixed-point-size, "the integer-size or fraction-size shall be greater than zero" requires at least one of the two, not both: NUMERIC*.5 and NUMERIC*3. are valid, NUMERIC*0.0 is rejected. The integer of a fixed-field-count must be greater than zero on its own, and string-field-size too. | l.7460, l.7463, l.7464, l.7466 |
| 11.3.2 | Two different record-setters in one file control | A given control-item appears at most once in a control (11.3.2 l.7471-7472, 11.4.2 l.7993-7997, 11.5.2 l.8504-8507), and the record-setters are one alternative of the production of a control-item, so two record-setters, even different ones (PRINT #1, BEGIN, END), make the program invalid and it is rejected at load. Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-04. | l.7471-7472, l.7993-7997, l.8504-8507 |
| 11.3.4.3 | MARGIN MAXNUM is a valid margin for a channel | "A margin of MAXNUM indicates that a record may be arbitrarily large": MAXNUM is a valid margin index (it evaluates greater than zero), so a SET MARGIN MAXNUM on a file channel is accepted, not a 4007. | l.7608-7609 |
| 11.3.4.9 | MAT WRITE # on a DISPLAY file | It is equivalent to MAT PRINT #: one line per array row in print-zone format, with an empty line between arrays and between planes of a 3-D array. | l.7685-7690 |
| 11.3.4.9 | MAT WRITE / MAT REWRITE / MAT REPLACE #n, RECORD r (or KEY k$) on a RELATIVE or KEYED DISPLAY file | One single record whose rows are separated by end-of-record; this extends the DISPLAY reading above and the standard does not state it explicitly. | l.7685-7690 |
| 11.4.2 | SAME after a PRINT # that completes a partial record | A PRINT with a trailing separator adds the partial record to the file (11.3.4.1 l.7563-7567), and the next PRINT without a record-setter appends to that same record and completes it (l.7570-7577). The record is a single file element, so the first file element touched by the completing PRINT is the whole record, and SAME (l.7240-7242) sets the pointer to it: LINE INPUT # with SAME returns the complete record. | l.7240-7242, l.7563-7579 |
| 11.4.4 | Order of 8101 and 8012 when a short record starts with an illegal datum | Data are transferred to the operands from left to right (l.8038-8042) and an exception during the transfer keeps the legal assignments already made (l.8051-8054). INPUT # A, B on a record whose only datum is not numeric therefore gives 8101 at A, before the shortage of data could be noticed at B; a record with one legal datum gives 8012 after A has received it. | l.8038-8054, l.8443-8446 |
| 11.4.4.3 | MAT INPUT # A(?) interrupted by an exception | The data of the input-reply are transferred to the vector from left to right. An illegal datum gives its exception; the legal data before it keep their values (l.8051-8054) and the upper bound becomes the subscript of the last element that received a datum (10.5.4.3 l.6014-6017). With more data than the original size of the vector (l.6018-6020), the elements that fit receive their data and the first datum that does not fit gives 8013, as INPUT # with too many data for its variables does. | l.6008-6020, l.8040-8054, l.8451-8453 |
| 12.1.2 | Detached-handler defined inside an internal SUB or FUNCTION | A detached-handler may be defined inside an internal-proc-def: 12.1.2 l.8708-8710 says that a detached-handler referred to in a when-use-name-line within an internal-proc-def 'shall be defined in the same internal-proc-def', which only makes sense if a handler can live inside such a routine, although the productions of 9.1.2 and 9.2.2 list only a block* there. The interpreter accepts it (SUB S with WHEN EXCEPTION USE H and HANDLER H inside). Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-04. | l.8708-8710 |
| 12.1.2 | EXTYPE and EXLINE inside a routine body called from a handler | 12.1.2 l.8688-8692 says EXLINE and EXTYPE 'shall be invoked only within exception-handlers'. The interpreter reads 'invoked' as a run-time notion: the main program body rejects them lexically, but the body of an internal or external routine accepts them, because a helper routine called from a handler may legitimately inspect the exception (claim A-12.1.2-02). Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-05. | l.8688-8692 |
| 12.1.4 | Exception inside a handler whose when-use-block is nested in another when-block | An exception raised inside a handler whose when-use-block lies inside another when-block of the same unit is fatal, following the literal rule of 12.1.4 l.8873-8875 (an exception in a handler is not handled by the same handler's when-block). The alternative, that the outer handler takes it by the lexical propagation of the Remarks (l.8940-8947), is not adopted. Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-05. | l.8873-8875 |
| 12.1.4 | Leaving an exception-handler by EXIT FOR or EXIT DO | An EXIT FOR or EXIT DO in a handler, for a loop that contains the whole when-block, is accepted and leaves the handler with no further effect, as an end-when-line does. The four means of exiting listed in 12.1.4 describe the handler-return statements and are not stated as a restriction. | l.8818-8840 |
| 12.2.4 | Trace of the line that raises an exception which transfers control to a handler | The line whose execution raises an exception that is handled by an exception-handler interrupts the sequential order of execution (4.2.4 case 2), so with tracing on it is reported together with the line-number of the next line to be executed: the first line of the handler, since the use-line (or the handler-line of a detached handler) is not executed (40 -> 70 for CAUSE EXCEPTION 7 on line 40 and a handler whose use-line is 60). The text of 12.2.4 does not distinguish the cause of the interruption. Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-03. | l.9117-9121, l.1365-1371, l.8790-8806 |
| 12.2.4 | Spelling of the traced variable name (upper or lower case) | Lower-case and upper-case letters are the same identifier (4.4.4), so a trace report that names the variable in the canonical upper-case form satisfies 'the name of the variable traced, as that name lexically appears in the statement': LET abc = 7 is reported as ABC=7. The wording distinguishes the name from its value or position, not its case. Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-03. | l.9139-9143, l.1520-1523, l.9163 |
| 12.2.4 | Format of the value in a trace report | The contents of the trace report are implementation-defined (12.2.4 l.9138, Appendix C 12.2 item 2) as long as they include the variable name and its value: the value is reported in the form of the assigned value, without the PRINT-style sign space, trailing space and point of a printed number (LET Q = 2.9999999999 is reported as Q=3, while PRINT Q gives ' 3. '). | l.9138-9143, l.9163 |
| 13.1.4 | When the display surface is already clear for SET DEVICE WINDOW and SET DEVICE VIEWPORT | The surface counts as not clear only when a graphic output statement has drawn on it since the start of the program or the last clear; text written by PRINT does not count, so a device set-statement after PRINT alone requests no clear. When a clear is requested, the macOS application clears the text output too, as CLEAR does (13.2.1). | l.9316-9318, l.9330-9331, l.9532-9535 |
| 13.5.2 | Declared and defined picture of the same name | 'No more than one picture of a given name declared or defined' counts pictures, not statements: a DECLARE PICTURE and the definition it announces are one picture, but two DECLARE PICTURE of the same name are two declarations and are rejected. | l.10511-10512 |
| 13.5.5 | SHEAR(A) with OPTION ANGLE DEGREES at an odd multiple of 90 degrees | SHEAR(A) maps (x,y) to (x+y*tan(A),y); tan(90 degrees) is mathematical infinity, so the exception of 5.4.5 is raised (1003), consistently with TAN(90). Decision of the project owner, 2026-11-03. | l.10673-10681, l.2084-2085 |
| 15.1.4 | Precision P of a NUMERIC*E field | P = 18: at least the first 18 significant digits of a value moved to a field of size E are retained exactly, and the field serializes to 25 bytes ([+/-]X.<17 digits>e[+/-]NN) in INTERNAL/NATIVE records (interno; the standard leaves P implementation-defined). | l.12273-12278 |
| 15.1.4 | Significant digits of a negated constant used as a print item (D-15.1-4) | A leading sign in an expression belongs to the numeric-expression (5.3.2 prod. 2, sign? term), so -12345678901234567 is an expression whose primary is the constant, not a signed numeric-constant (5.1.2 prod. 2 applies to data such as READ/INPUT). Its significant digits are therefore implementation-defined (l.12250-12259). The implementation materializes the result with the default fixed-point-size limited to P = 18 digits in all: under FIXED*8.2, PRINT -1234567 gives -1234567.00, PRINT -12345678901234567 gives -12345678901234567.0 (scale 1) and PRINT -123456789012345678 gives -123456789012345678 (scale 0). The constants without sign print their written digits (l.12188-12203). | l.12188-12203, l.12250-12259 |
| 15.2.2 | ARITHMETIC agreement between program-units joined by CHAIN, and the ordering rule of OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED | 15.2.2 l.12354-12357 requires only that the ARITHMETIC options of the two program-units agree in type (both DECIMAL, both NATIVE or both FIXED), not in fixed-point precision: CHAIN from FIXED*4.2 to FIXED*8.2 runs without 4303, while NATIVE vs DECIMAL raises 4303 both ways. The ordering rule of 15.1.2 l.12145-12148 applies to numeric expressions, variables and NUMERIC declare-statements of the program-unit, not to the numeric parameters of the program-name-line (the first line), so a FIXED program with numeric program parameters is conforming. | l.12354-12357, l.12145-12148 |

## 5. Implementation-defined values

Appendix C of the standard lists the features whose value each implementation chooses; the claimed items and their values are:

| Clause | Claim ID | Module | Item | Value | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.3 | D-2.3-1 | core | How syntactically illegal constructs are interpreted, a point Appendix C subsection 2.3 leaves to each implementation. | They are rejected at load time: the program is never executed, every syntax error found is listed on stderr and the CLI exits with status 1 (measured: '10 PARALLEL' is rejected with a load-time syntax error because the real-time module is not implemented). | PRG-0013 |
| 2.3 | D-2.3-2 | core | Format of error messages, a point Appendix C subsection 2.3 leaves to each implementation. | Load-time errors are reported on stderr as the header 'Error loading the program:' followed by one line per error '  ERROR <code>: line N[:C] - <msg>' (syntax errors carry the code E-SYNTAX, e.g. '  ERROR E-SYNTAX: line 20:7 - Syntax error: ...') plus the closing line '  Error processing the source code'; exit status 1. Load-time warnings (the 1010 of a fixed-point-size above P) go to stderr under 'Warnings while loading the program:' as '  WARNING <code>: line N:C - <msg>' and the program runs. The messages are in English. Measured with the CLI (the FBCS harness only asserts the rejection, not the text). | PRG-0013 |
| 2.4 | D-2.4-1 | core | Format of exception messages, a point Appendix C subsection 2.4 leaves to each implementation (the report must at least identify the code and the line, l.619-621). | An uncaught nonfatal exception prints on STDOUT 'Warning <code>: line N:C - <msg> (<clause>)' and execution continues (exit 0), e.g. 'Warning 3101: line 20:10 - Uninitialized numeric-variable 'X' (5.2)'; measured with the CLI: stderr stays empty, and if a PRINT with a pending end-of-line was in progress the warning is interleaved into that output line. An uncaught fatal exception prints 'ERROR <code>: line N[:C] - <msg>' on stderr and terminates the program (exit 1), e.g. 'ERROR 3001: line 20:10 - Division by zero'; load-time errors also go to stderr (D-2.3-2). All the texts of the CLI are in English since 2026-11-11. Measured with the CLI. A nonfatal exception raised in the middle of a PRINT (TAB, USING$, an uninitialized variable) prints its report at once, before the rest of the line, as the NBS test P008 requires (an X in column 1 after the system message); only the 8203 of a PRINT USING without a final separator is reported after the end-of-line of the statement. | PRT-0001, PRT-0157 |
| 2.4 | D-2.4-2 | core | Hardware-dependent exceptions and how resource-constraint exceptions out of the standard's fixed recovery are handled, a point Appendix C subsection 2.4 leaves to each implementation. | No hardware-dependent exceptions beyond the standard's are defined. Underflow policy (1500 series, all nonfatal, value 0 supplied): 1502, 1503, 1504, 1506 and 1507 are raised and, uncaught, print a Warning line (measured: LET A = 1E-300*1E-300 -> Warning 1502; EXP(-800) -> Warning 1503; VAL('1E-400') -> Warning 1504; DATA 1E-400 -> Warning 1506; INPUT of 1E-400 -> Warning 1507); 1501 is catchable in a WHEN block (EXTYPE 1501, NUM-0006) but prints no uncaught Warning (LET X = 1E-401 yields 0 silently); 1505 and 1508 are never raised (E-1505/E-1508 not-applicable). Overflow raises fatal 1002/1003 in expressions and functions. The depth of procedure invocation (CALL, function invocation and GOSUB together) is limited to 100000 levels: the invocation that would exceed it raises the fatal implementation exception -10011 before entering, catchable in a when-block (EXTYPE -110011 when propagated out of the procedure, 12.1.4 l.8909-8913; EXC-0264). | NUM-0006, NUM-0032, NUM-0058, STR-0040, PRT-0025, PRT-0047, EXC-0264 |
| 2.4 | D-2.4-3 | core | Order of exception detection in a line, a point Appendix C subsection 2.4 leaves to each implementation. | When a single statement raises several exceptions, the first one in evaluation order is detected and reported; operands are evaluated right-to-left (D-5.3-1), so in 'PRINT SQR(-1) + 1/0' the division by zero (3001) is reported and in 'PRINT 1/0 + SQR(-1)' the square root of a negative (3005) is reported. Measured with the CLI. | NUM-0033 |
| 3.2 | D-3.2-1 | core | The semantic rules for native data (collating sequence, precision) that the definition of 'native' in subsection 3.2 leaves implementation-defined (Appendix C, subsection 3.2). | Native data follows the host model: strings are sequences of Latin-1 characters, one position each (LEN of 'ñ' is 1, D-4.1-1), the native collating sequence is character-code order identical to STANDARD (D-4.1.4-1, D-6.6-1), CHR$/ORD use character codes 0..255 (D-6.4-1, D-6.4-2), and NATIVE arithmetic is backed by binary64 and quantized to 8 significant digits (D-5.6-3: fpScale 8; measured NUM-0243: 1/3*3 - 1 = -1E-8 and 1/3 - .33333333 = 0), which exceeds the 6 significant digits the standard requires (NUM-0082: 1/3 within 5E-7, MAXNUM > 1E+38, EPS(0) < 2E-38); values are printed with d = 8 digits under NATIVE as under DECIMAL (D-10.3-2). | PRG-0023, STR-0059, NUM-0082, NUM-0243 |
| 4.1.4 | D-4.1.4-1 | core | Coding used for the native collating sequence under OPTION COLLATE NATIVE, which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | OPTION COLLATE NATIVE orders strings by character code (ASCII, then the Latin-1 other-characters 128..255), identical to STANDARD for all input; no locale-aware collation is implemented. | PRG-0023 |
| 4.1.6 | D-4.1-1 | core | Meaning of other-characters beyond ASCII: what they do in strings, in input data, in files and in CHR$ values, which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | Other-characters are the Latin-1 (ISO/IEC 8859-1) characters at ordinal positions 128..255, one position per character: LEN, substrings and MAXLEN count characters (the e-acute has LEN 1), and they are accepted inside quoted strings, in unquoted data (INPUT, DATA, DISPLAY files) at any position, and in remarks. The program text is UTF-8 and is converted to Latin-1 on loading; a character outside Latin-1 (U+0100 and above) anywhere in the source, comments included, is a load error (E-NOT-LATIN1, with line and column), and one in input data or in a DISPLAY file is exception 8102 (INPUT, LINE INPUT, MAT INPUT) or 8105 (file); console and graphic text leave as UTF-8; DISPLAY files (sequential, stream, relative and keyed, keys included) are stored in UTF-8 on disk with RECSIZE and MARGIN counted in characters, while INTERNAL and NATIVE files keep the Latin-1 bytes unconverted. CHR$(n) yields the character at position n for 0..255 (ORD(CHR$(233)) = 233 and ORD("é") = 233); ORD rejects a string of more than one character with exception 4003. UCASE$ and LCASE$ convert every Latin-1 letter (sharp s and y-diaeresis have no one-character counterpart and stay), and strings compare by character code ("z" < "ñ"). The standard character set has 256 characters: the 128 ASCII characters plus 128 additional other-characters in ordinal positions 128..255 (Tabla 8 l.12768-12770 leaves the number implementation-defined; here 128), so CHR$(127.5) rounds to 128 and is legal (no 4002). | PRG-0025, PRG-0026, PRG-0080, PRG-0081, STR-0093, STR-0094 |
| 4.2.2 | D-4.2-1 | core | How the end of a line is recognised (carriage return, return plus line feed, end of record, ...), which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | End-of-line is LF (0x0A); a CRLF pair is also accepted (the CR is discarded); a lone CR is not an end-of-line (lexer error). PRG-0034 reads its own source back line by line. | PRG-0034 |
| 4.2.2 | D-4.2-2 | core | Actual maximum physical line length accepted, which Appendix C lists as implementation-defined even though 132 characters is the limit the standard states. | The maximum physical line length accepted is exactly 132 characters (STD §4.2.2 l.1329): a 132-character line is accepted (PRG-0035) and a 133-character line is rejected at load with E-LINE-TOO-LONG (PRG-0033). | PRG-0035 |
| 4.2.4 | D-4.2-4 | core | How the program designator of a CHAIN relates to the program name, which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | The CHAIN designator is a file path only; the PROGRAM name of the target is not compared with the designator (measured: CHAIN "tgt" ran tgt.BAS declaring PROGRAM OtherName). A missing file raises fatal exception 10005, which PRG-0036 verifies via WHEN/USE and EXTYPE. | PRG-0036 |
| 4.4.6 | D-4.4-1 | core | Extra limits an operating system may put on the length and form of identifiers of procedures compiled separately from the main program, which Appendix C leaves to each implementation. | No separate compilation exists (all procedures live in one source file), so the OS imposes no extra limits on procedure identifiers; external-sub names of 31 characters (and longer) are accepted. | PRG-0059 |
| 5.1 | D-5.1-1 | core | The precision and the range kept for numeric constants (Appendix C, subsection 5.1) are chosen by the implementation, within the minimums fixed by section 5.1.4. | Numeric constants are held as exact decimals up to 18 significant digits (printed with 8 significant digits (d = 8, D-10.3-2) under DECIMAL and NATIVE alike); magnitude range EPS(0)=2.2250738585073E-308 to MAXNUM=1.7976931348623157E+308 under DECIMAL (D-5.4-2). | NUM-0007 |
| 5.2 | D-5.2-1 | core | The value every numeric variable holds when execution starts (Appendix C, subsection 5.2) is chosen by the implementation. | Every numeric variable starts at 0; a read before any assignment also raises the nonfatal exception 3101 (EXTYPE 3101) and supplies 0. The same holds for an array element read by MAT PRINT, MAT PRINT USING, MAT WRITE or MAT GRAPH: the statement supplies 0, completes, and raises 3101 once (3102 for a string array). | NUM-0014, ARR-0210, ARR-0211, ARR-0212, ARR-0213, ARR-0214 |
| 5.3 | D-5.3-1 | core | Beyond the fixed precedence and left-to-right grouping rules, the order in which the parts of a numeric expression are evaluated (Appendix C, subsection 5.3) is chosen by the implementation. | Operands of an operator are evaluated right-to-left in source order (with a side-effecting internal FUNCTION INC, INC(0)*10+INC(0) yields 21, i.e. the right call is evaluated first); grouping itself stays left-to-right per 5.3.4. | NUM-0033 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-1 | core | The accuracy with which built-in numeric functions are evaluated (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) is chosen by the implementation. | Under DECIMAL every numeric function (SQR, EXP, LOG, LOG10, LOG2, SIN, COS, TAN, SEC, CSC, COT, ATN, ANGLE, ASIN, ACOS, SINH, COSH, TANH) and the power operator are computed in decimal with 34 working digits and rounded once to the 18-digit result, so each is the true value rounded to 18 digits (error at most 5 units in the 19th digit, the 5.6.4 bound for m = 17; measured on 2026-11-08); under NATIVE they are computed in binary64 and quantized to 8 significant digits; values print with 8 significant digits (d = 8, D-10.3-2). | NUM-0059 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-2 | core | The values of MAXNUM and of EPS (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) are chosen by the implementation. | MAXNUM = 1.7976931348623157E+308 and EPS(0) = sigma = 2.2250738585073E-308 under DECIMAL (the IEEE-754 binary64 limits; DBL_MIN kept with 14 digits); under NATIVE MAXNUM = 1.7976931E+308 and EPS(0) = 2.2250739E-308 (DBL_MAX and DBL_MIN quantized to 8 digits); under FIXED *i.f, MAXNUM is the largest value of P digits and EPS(0) = 10^-f (.001 under *8.3), the smallest positive value representable in the mode. | NUM-0060 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-3 | core | The pseudorandom sequence from which RND draws its values (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) is chosen by the implementation. | RND draws from the C library rand() sequence seeded with 1 when RANDOMIZE is not executed (first values .417022, .99718481, .72032449, .93255736, 1.1438108E-4, printed to d = 8 digits, D-10.3-2); RANDOMIZE reseeds from the system clock. | NUM-0061 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-4 | core | Whether a calendar and a clock are available to DATE and TIME (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) is chosen by the implementation. | A calendar and a clock are available: DATE returns the YYDDD of the local date (26305 on 2026-11-01) and TIME returns seconds since local midnight (0 <= TIME < 86400); neither yields -1 on this host. | NUM-0062 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-5 | core | The time zone used by DATE and TIME (Appendix C, subsection 5.4) is chosen by the implementation. | The host local time zone (Europe/Madrid: CET UTC+1 in winter, CEST UTC+2 in summer) is used for DATE and TIME. | NUM-0063 |
| 5.4 | D-5.4-6 | core | Tie-break of rounding to the nearest when the discarded portion is exactly half (the text fixes ROUND(X,N) = INT(X*10^N+.5)/10^N at 5.4.4 l.2015-2017 and suggests INT(X+0.5) at 3.2 l.1012-1017, but does not fix the tie of the i/f/e-format output of 10.4.4.3 l.5722/l.5725-5727). | Half-up, unique everywhere (decision of the project owner, 2026-11-02): ROUND and the i/f/e-format items of PRINT USING round the magnitude half-up over the exact decimal value (1.25 -> 1.3 at one decimal, .125 -> .13, 1.005 -> 1.01, 2.5 -> 3). ROUND on negative values follows the normative formula INT(X*10^N+.5)/10^N (ROUND(-1.25,1) = -1.2). | NUM-0103, PRT-0156 |
| 5.6 | D-5.6-1 | core | The precision and range of numeric values in general (Appendix C, subsection 5.6) are chosen by the implementation. | Default arithmetic is decimal floating point with a documented precision m = 17 significant digits (what the operations + - * / and the constants meet, error at most 5 units in the 19th digit); values are held with an 18-digit mantissa and EPS reflects that representation (EPS(1) = 1E-17); range EPS(0)=2.2250738585073E-308 .. MAXNUM=1.7976931348623157E+308, printed with 8 significant digits (d = 8, D-10.3-2). The supplied functions and the power operator meet this precision too (A-5.6.4-FN1). | NUM-0080 |
| 5.6 | D-5.6-2 | core | The precision and range of the decimal floating-point arithmetic (Appendix C, subsection 5.6) are chosen by the implementation. | OPTION ARITHMETIC DECIMAL: exact decimal floating point, documented precision m = 17, 18-digit mantissa in variables and intermediates (EPS(1) = 1E-17), range 2.2250738585073E-308 .. 1.7976931348623157E+308; 0.1+0.2 = 0.3 exactly. | NUM-0081 |
| 5.6 | D-5.6-3 | core | The precision and range of native arithmetic (Appendix C, subsection 5.6) are chosen by the implementation. | OPTION ARITHMETIC NATIVE: same binary64-backed values quantized to 8 significant digits (fpScale 8); range 2.2250739E-308 .. 1.7976931E+308; observed precision 8 digits (at least 6 required). | NUM-0082, NUM-0243 |
| 5.6 | D-5.6-4 | core | The accuracy of numeric expression evaluation (Appendix C, subsection 5.6) is chosen by the implementation. | With m = 17: constants, the operations + - * / and every numeric function and power err at most 5 units in the 19th significant digit and are exact when the true result fits in 18 digits (0.1+0.2 = 0.3). The transcendental functions are computed in decimal with 34 working digits and rounded once to 18 digits; the measurement of 2026-11-08 gives m = 17 for all of them, in radians and degrees, including the ill-conditioned zones. | NUM-0083, NUM-0281 |
| 6.2 | D-6.2-1 | core | Value held by every string variable when execution begins, before any assignment. | Null string: reading a string variable before assignment raises nonfatal 3102 (catchable); uncaught, a warning is issued and the value used is the null string (LEN 0). | STR-0013 |
| 6.2 | D-6.2-2 | core | Default maximum length of a string variable that has no declared length limit (the default string length limit, at least 132). | The effective limit of 1E9 characters (one limit for every string): MAXLEN of an undeclared string variable returns 1000000000, above the required minimum of 132. A string expression whose result would be longer raises the fatal 1051 (REPEAT$, concatenation, substring assignment; E-1051) and a string-array expression the fatal 1052 (MAT concatenation, 7.3.5; E-1052); the length is checked before the string is built. | STR-0014, STR-0091 |
| 6.4 | D-6.4-1 | core | CHR$ results for the native character set. | CHR$(M) returns the character with code M of the Latin-1 set (CHR$(65)="A", CHR$(48)="0", CHR$(233)="é"); under COLLATE NATIVE the native set applies. | STR-0056 |
| 6.4 | D-6.4-2 | core | ORD results for the native character set. | ORD under the native set returns the character code (ASCII, or Latin-1 for 128..255): ORD("A")=65, ORD("a")=97, ORD("5")=53, ORD(" ")=32, ORD("é")=233. | STR-0057 |
| 6.4 | D-6.4-3 | core | Whether a calendar and a clock are available to DATE$ and TIME$. | Calendar and clock are available: DATE$ returns the host date as YYYYMMDD and TIME$ the host time as HH:MM:SS; the no-device values "00000000" and "99:99:99" are unreachable here. | STR-0058 |
| 6.6 | D-6.6-1 | core | Collating sequence used under OPTION COLLATE NATIVE. | Ordering by character code (ASCII, then the Latin-1 other-characters 128..255), which coincides with Table 8 over the ASCII range 0..127. | STR-0059 |
| 6.6 | D-6.6-2 | core | Maximum length of a declared string variable that has no length-max (the implementation-defined default). | The effective limit of 1E9 characters: MAXLEN of a declared variable without length-max returns 1000000000, above the required 132. A length-max above that limit (DECLARE STRING A$*2000000000, also in a string-type, a string array, a DEF or a FUNCTION) is rejected at load with E-STRING-LENGTH-MAX-TOO-LARGE, because the length-max guarantees that values of that length can be stored (6.6.4 l.2886-2896; decision of the project owner, 2026-11-12; measured with the CLI). | STR-0060, STR-0095 |
| 7.1.4 | D-7.1-1 | core | Default maximum length of an element of a string array when neither the declaration nor the string type sets a length limit. | The effective limit of 1E9 characters: MAXLEN of a string array declared without length-max returns 1000000000 and strings of 200 characters are stored whole (far above the required minimum of 132). | ARR-0137 |
| 7.2.4.3 | D-7.2.4-1 | core | Which bounds an explicit redim-bounds (index TO index) fixes on the destination array of a MAT assignment with an array function (ZER, CON, IDN, NUL$), where 7.2.4.3 and 7.2.4.1 admit two readings. | Agreed interpretation of 7.2.4 (decision of the project owner, 2026-11-02): the redim-bounds are the lower and upper bounds of the array-value only (7.2.4.3 l.3258-3263); the destination array is resized as 7.2.4.1 orders (it keeps its old lower bound and its new upper bound is old lower plus new size minus one, l.3210-3214): DIM A(5,5) + MAT A = ZER(0 TO 1, 2 TO 3) leaves A with bounds 1..2, 1..2. A single index (ZER(3)) is unchanged: upper bound only, current default lower bound in effect. MAT READ with a redim is different: it fixes both bounds of the destination (10.5.4.1 l.5948-5953). | ARR-0162, ARR-0201, ARR-0202 |
| 7.2.4.4 | D-7.2-1 | core | Value produced by INV for a singular matrix, which Appendix C leaves to the implementation (the exception 3009 case is claim E-3009). | No value is produced: INV of a singular matrix raises fatal exception 3009 (claim E-3009), so the Appendix C value never occurs. | ARR-0180 |
| 9.1.4.1 | D-9.1-1 | core | Maximum length of a string parameter or string array parameter of a function that has no length limit. | No effective limit: a function string parameter without a length limit holds any string up to the default string-variable limit, which is the effective limit of 1E9 characters (D-6.2-2); observed a 40000-character string passed unchanged. | SEG-0222, SEG-0347 |
| 9.1.4.2 | D-9.1-2 | core | Value returned by a function that ended without any assignment to its name. | Numeric 0 (empty string for a string function): the policy for uninitialized variables, with a nonfatal 3101/3102 warning, in EVERY invocation that exits before assigning its name (never the value left by a previous invocation, also under recursion; SEG-0227 calls the function five times, SEG-0397 covers a string function and a recursive one). | SEG-0227, SEG-0397 |
| 9.1.4.3 | D-9.1-3 | core | Initial values of the local variables and arrays of an external function on each invocation. | Numeric 0 and empty string on each invocation (the uninitialized-variable policy, nonfatal warnings 3101/3102). | SEG-0239 |
| 9.2.4.1 | D-9.2-1 | core | Maximum length of a string parameter or string array parameter without a length limit when it is passed by value. | No effective limit: a by-value string parameter without a length limit holds any string up to the default string-variable limit, the effective 1E9 characters (D-6.2-2); observed a 40000-character string. | SEG-0279 |
| 9.2.4.1 | D-9.2-2 | core | Effect, inside the subprogram, of redimensioning an array when an element of that same array is also passed as an argument. | The parameter keeps naming the element with the subscripts evaluated on entry, checked against the current bounds: if the redimensioned array still has that element the parameter is that element; if not, a reference to the parameter raises 2001 (subscript out of bounds). | SEG-0170, SEG-0171 |
| 9.2.4.2 | D-9.2-3 | core | Initial values of the variables and arrays of a subprogram that are not formal parameters, on each invocation of an external subprogram. | Numeric 0 and empty string on each invocation of an external subprogram (uninitialized-variable policy; warnings 3101/3102). | SEG-0288 |
| 9.3.4 | D-9.3-1 | core | How a program designator in CHAIN is associated with a program. | The designator is a file name resolved against the current working directory of the interpreter process; the named file must contain the chained BASIC program. | SEG-0304 |
| 9.3.4 | D-9.3-2 | core | Whether upper-case and lower-case letters are equivalent in a program designator. | Case is not significant on this build's default macOS APFS volume (resolution follows the host file system): CHAIN 'mixedcase.bas' runs the file written as MixedCase.BAS. | SEG-0305 |
| 9.3.4 | D-9.3-3 | core | Initial values of the variables of a chained-to program. | Numeric variables start at 0 and string variables at empty (the uninitialized-variable policy, warnings 3101/3102); observed inside the chained-to program. | SEG-0306 |
| 9.3.6 | D-9.3-4 | core | Which program reports the exceptions 4301, 4302 and 4303 of a chain-statement, and whether the chained-from program's WHEN can intercept them. | The interpreter reports them itself (as the chained-from side) as FATAL exceptions localized at the CHAIN statement; they are NOT interceptable by a WHEN handler of the chained-from program. STD §9.3.6 l.4927-4932 allows the chained-from program, the chained-to program or an intermediate system program to report them, so no WHEN interception is promised; this implementation chooses the interpreter, fatal. | SEG-0307, SEG-0308, SEG-0310, SEG-0313 |
| 10.2.4.1 | D-10.2-1 | core | The built-in input-prompt shown when no PROMPT specifier is given (Appendix C, subsection 10.2 item 1). | No input-prompt is output in batch mode (stdin is not a terminal); interactive mode would use the recommended '? ' of l.5288, which the FBCS runner cannot drive. | PRT-0048 |
| 10.2.4.1 | D-10.2-2 | core | How batch mode asks the external source for an input-reply (Appendix C, subsection 10.2 item 2). | In batch mode each input-reply (or line-input-reply) is read as one line of standard input, without any prompt output. The text of a PROMPT specifier is still written in batch mode (INPUT PROMPT "Dime: ": A writes Dime: before reading), and the reply is not echoed (measured with the CLI). | PRT-0049 |
| 10.2.4.1 | D-10.2-3 | core | Minimum, maximum and resolution of TIMEOUT expressions and ELAPSED time-inquiries (Appendix C, subsection 10.2 item 3). | TIMEOUT accepts any fractional value >= 0 (0 is accepted, negative raises 8402); ELAPSED returns positive fractional seconds because a clock is provided. | PRT-0050 |
| 10.3.4 | D-10.3-1 | core | Effect when a function called during a PRINT prints to the same device (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 1). | The function's output goes to the same device in evaluation order, sharing the columnar position: PRINT "a"; F(1); "b" with a function that does PRINT "[in]"; writes a[in] 1 b on one line, and when the function ends its own line (PRINT "SIDE", PRT-0079) the outer PRINT continues on the next one. | PRT-0079 |
| 10.3.4.1 | D-10.3-2 | core | Significance width d used when printing numeric representations (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 2). | d = 8 significant digits (decision of the project owner, 2026-11-02; zone width 17 = d+e+6 with e = 3, l.5444-5446). | PRT-0080 |
| 10.3.4.1 | D-10.3-3 | core | Exrad width e used when printing numeric representations (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 3). | e = 3 exrad digits (decision of the project owner, 2026-11-02; 1E100 prints 1.E+100 and MAXNUM 1.7976931E+308, exrad of 3 digits, STD 10.3.4.1 (5) l.5405-5412 "one to e digits"). | PRT-0081, PRT-0155 |
| 10.3.4.3 | D-10.3-4 | core | Effect of characters outside the standard printable set on the columnar position (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 4). | Every emitted character, including control characters, advances the columnar position by one. | PRT-0082 |
| 10.3.4.3 | D-10.3-5 | core | Margin in effect before any SET MARGIN (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 5). | The default margin before any SET MARGIN is 132. | PRT-0083 |
| 10.3.4.3 | D-10.3-6 | core | Number of print zones per line and their width before any SET ZONEWIDTH (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 6). | Default zone width 17 = d+e+6 (d = 8, e = 3; l.5444-5446) on the default margin 132: 8 print zones per line (cols 1,18,35,52,69,86,103,120), the last one 13 columns wide (120-132). | PRT-0084 |
| 10.3.6 | D-10.3-7 | core | Whether the trailing space of a printed number is emitted when it would push the column past the margin (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 7). | The trailing space of a printed number is always emitted; when the whole number field would cross the margin, an end-of-line is generated first (l.5484), so the space is never dropped. | PRT-0085 |
| 10.3.6 | D-10.3-8 | core | Case of the E letter used in scaled numeric output (Appendix C, subsection 10.3 item 8). | The E of scaled numeric output is uppercase. | PRT-0086 |
| 10.5.4.2 | D-10.5-1 | core | Effect of resupplying input to an array that was resized after data was already assigned to it (Appendix C, subsection 10.5 item 1). | On resupply to a redimensioned array the resupplied reply overwrites the array from its first element; the final contents are those of the last reply (SIZE re-set to that reply count). | PRT-0138 |
| 11 | D-11-1 | files | The effect of file-organization and record-type combinations beyond those of the core and enhanced modules is implementation-defined. | Unlisted organization/record-type combinations are accepted and processed according to the record type. STREAM+DISPLAY: PRINT # writes one line per statement, as for SEQUENTIAL+DISPLAY (so PRINT #n: 1, 2, 3 writes ONE line with print zones, 10.3.4.3, and reading it back with READ #n: X into a numeric variable raises 8101, 11.4.5.3 l.8430-8431, because the zone-padded text is not a single numeric-constant), but reading follows the stream rule of 11.4.4.8 (l.8224-8235): INPUT #, READ # and MAT INPUT # take their data from the sequence of data in the file, line boundaries are not significant (a line with too few data does not raise 8012: the next line supplies the rest; only the end of the file raises 8011) and the data left over from the current line are the next file elements; LINE INPUT # and MAT LINE INPUT # return the unread rest of the current line as it is, spaces included, when data are pending, and the next line otherwise; MAT INPUT X(?) takes the pending data of the current line or, if none, the data of the next line that has any. STREAM+NATIVE needs a TEMPLATE like any NATIVE file and follows the same stream rule: there are no records, so READ # takes the next fields of the file whatever the previous statement read, a template longer than the data left raises 8011 at the end of the file, and 8012/8013 never occur. Files written by builds before 2026-11-09 are not read: no released version wrote them. | FIL-0152, FIL-0601 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-1 | files | The maximum channel number is implementation-defined (the standard only requires it to be at least 99). | 255 (channels 0..255; channel 256 raises 7001). | FIL-0153 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-10 | files | The length of records of type INTERNAL and NATIVE is implementation-defined. | INTERNAL records are stored as typed tag+payload values (tag u8: 0x01 double LE, 0x02 FIXED scaled, 0x03 string u32len+bytes, 0x04 exact DECIMAL); NATIVE records as fixed template fields; record length varies with the values. | FIL-0160 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-11 | files | When RECSIZE omits the LENGTH index, the maximum record length of the file is implementation-defined. | MAXNUM: no effective limit on record length (ASK RECSIZE reports VARIABLE). | FIL-0055 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-12 | files | The DATUM ask-value for file organizations other than STREAM INTERNAL is implementation-defined. | 'UNKNOWN' for a SEQUENTIAL DISPLAY file (null string on an inactive channel); DATUM is only well-defined for STREAM INTERNAL files. | FIL-0161 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-13 | files | The NAME ask-value returned for channel zero is implementation-defined. | The null string. | FIL-0162 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-14 | files | The meaning of the implementation-defined file-access failure codes 7101 through 7199 is implementation-defined. | 7107 = file does not exist; 7108 = invalid file name, raised by an OPEN whose NAME is the empty string (a name of spaces is not empty), for every ACCESS and ORGANIZATION (11.1.5 l.7069-7072). | FIL-0163, FIL-0564 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-15 | files | The maximum length of a key in a KEYED file is implementation-defined. | At least 10000 characters; no limit observed. | FIL-0164 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-2 | files | Whether file names differing only in letter case denote the same file or different files is implementation-defined. | Case-insensitive on the host filesystem: names differing only in letter case denote the same file. | FIL-0154 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-3 | files | Opening a file that is already open has implementation-defined consequences. | Opening an already-open file on another channel succeeds; both channels then share the file. | FIL-0155 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-4 | files | How many nonzero channels beyond the required minimum may be active simultaneously is implementation-defined. | At least 10 nonzero channels may be active simultaneously (observed 10 of 10). | FIL-0156 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-5 | files | Whether a file closed and later reopened with different organization, record type or record size remains accessible is implementation-defined. | The file remains accessible when reopened with a different organization or record type (observed RELATIVE and INTERNAL reopens of a SEQUENTIAL DISPLAY file). | FIL-0157 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-6 | files | For INTERNAL and NATIVE files, whether a reopen under a different ARITHMETIC option keeps the file accessible is implementation-defined. | An INTERNAL file reopened under OPTION ARITHMETIC NATIVE remains accessible with its contents preserved (observed 1.5 read back unchanged). | FIL-0158 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-7 | files | Accessing an INTERNAL or NATIVE file from another program unit under a different ARITHMETIC option has implementation-defined results. | Access under a different ARITHMETIC option works (observed reopen of an INTERNAL file under OPTION ARITHMETIC NATIVE, contents preserved). | FIL-0158 |
| 11.1 | D-11.1-8 | files | The means a user employs to keep file contents unchanged between runs of a program is implementation-defined. | Ordinary files in the working directory persist between runs of the program; no special means is needed. | FIL-0159 |

| 12.1 | D-12.1-1 | core | Which EXTYPE value a local enhancement assigns to each of its own exceptions (Appendix C, subsection 12.1 item 1). | Negative EXTYPE values identify local-enhancement exceptions: this implementation uses -99000, -99001, -99004 and -99993 for its internal errors; when such a value is propagated out of a procedure it becomes -100000 plus the original value (e.g. -100042 for -42). | EXC-0060 |
| 12.1 | D-12.1-2 | core | The precise format of the string that EXTEXT$ returns (Appendix C, subsection 12.1 item 2). | EXTEXT$(n) rounds n to an integer and returns the Table 9 message text in the form description plus parenthesized clause list, e.g. EXTEXT$(1001) is the string Overflow in evaluating numeric-constant (5.1, 15.1); for a number that is not a standard system exception (e.g. 2002) it returns the null string. | 12.2 | D-12.2-1 | core | What the debugging system allows the user to do at a break point, including how execution continues or ends (Appendix C, subsection 12.2 item 1). | No interactive debugger in the CLI: an uncaught BREAK with debugging active prints a Warning 10007 line report and continues with the next line (exit 0); 10007 is nonfatal and may be caught in a WHEN block, where CONTINUE or RETRY resumes execution. | EXC-0062 |
| 12.2 | D-12.2-2 | core | The exact form of the trace reports (Appendix C, subsection 12.2 item 2). | Each trace report is a single line [TRACE] followed by the line number and the source text of that line, sent to the channel named in TRACE ... TO or to channel zero, e.g. [TRACE] 130 LET A = 42. A TRACE statement without channel-expression also writes 'Trace mode ON'/'Trace mode OFF' on channel zero; with TO #ch the reports go to that file (§12.2.4 l.9132-9136 fixes the destination; only the content is implementation-defined, l.9138) and no mode message is written to channel zero (decision of the project owner, 2026-11-03). The required reports have their own line: a control transfer as [TRACE] A -> B and the assignments of a line as [TRACE] N name=value, with the evaluated subscripts of an array element (C(3)=5), every element of a MAT assignment and string values in quotes; the name is spelled as it appears in the statement that assigns it (LET w = 20 reports w=20; §12.2.4 l.9125-9131). | EXC-0063, EXC-0081, EXC-0082, EXC-0265 |

| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-1 | fixed | The maximum precision P that bounds the decimal digits used to represent numeric values under fixed decimal is chosen by each implementation, but it must be at least 18 digits (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 1). | P = 18 decimal digits; FIX-0008 shows an 18-digit integer constant accepted under *18.0 and a 19-digit one raising 1001 | FIX-0008 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-2 | fixed | The precision attribute of the result of evaluating a fixed-decimal numeric expression or numeric supplied function is left to each implementation (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 2). | The result of an operation (+, -, *, /) is kept with up to P+2 = 20 significant digits and is not rounded to the default fixed-point-size of the OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED statement until it is assigned (FIX-0012: in *8.2, LET A = 1/3 stores .33, but the expression 1/3 is .33333333333333333333 and 1/3 = .33 is false). An expression printed as a print item shows the default fixed-point-size of the option (the recommendation of 15.1.6). The numeric supplied functions whose result is always an integer (EXTYPE, EXLINE, INT, IP, CEIL, SGN, LEN, POS, ORD, MAXLEN, MAXSIZE, SIZE, LBOUND, UBOUND, DATE) give a result of fraction-size 0 that prints like a constant: PRINT INT(2.5) prints 2, not 2.00; an expression built on them (INT(2.5) + 1) keeps the default size. Every intermediate result is checked: with A of 16 integer digits under *18.0, A*A/A raises 1002 at A*A although the final result would fit (l.12230-12234; measured with the CLI). | FIX-0012 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-3 | fixed | How accurately a fixed-decimal numeric expression or numeric supplied function is evaluated is left to each implementation (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 3). | Operations are computed in decimal with P+2 = 20 significant digits, two more than P, as 15.1.6 recommends, and the operands (constants, variables, intermediate results) keep their own precision (FIX-0013: in *8.2, 1/3*3 is .99999999999999999999, so 1/3*3 = 1 is false, while LET C = 1/3*3 stores 1.00 and 0.1+0.2 = .3 is true; FIX-0174) | FIX-0013 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-4 | fixed | The exact rule for which digits of a constant count as significant is left to each implementation (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 4). | Digits as written count as significant: a numeric-constant used as a print item prints exactly those digits, with 17 or 18 integer digits included when P >= 18 (l.12250-12259; FIX-0009/FIX-0015/FIX-0050). As an operand of an expression the constant keeps those digits (1.555 = 1.56 is false); when it is assigned it is rounded to the fixed-point-size of the variable, and when an expression or constant is converted by STR$ the text uses the default fixed-point-size of the program-unit OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED statement (FIX-0010 verifies this via STR$ in *9.9). A negated constant such as -12345678901234567 is not a numeric-constant in an expression: the sign belongs to the numeric-expression (5.3.2 prod. 2, 'sign? term') and the constant is its primary, so the digits of the result are implementation-defined (l.12250-12259). Here the result is materialized with the default size and limited to P = 18 digits in all: under FIXED*8.2, PRINT -1234567 gives -1234567.00, PRINT -12345678901234567 (17 integer digits) gives -12345678901234567.0 (scale 1) and PRINT -123456789012345678 (18 integer digits) gives -123456789012345678 (scale 0). FIX-0171 pins this. | FIX-0010, FIX-0171 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-5 | fixed | Whether an INTERNAL format file opened under one ARITHMETIC option can be accessed under another is left to each implementation; FIXED with a different default precision still counts as the same option (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 5). | INTERNAL files are accessible across different ARITHMETIC options: a datum written under FIXED reads back correctly under DECIMAL (FIX-0016) | FIX-0016 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-6 | fixed | Whether a NATIVE format file opened under one ARITHMETIC option can be accessed under another is left to each implementation (Appendix C, subsection 15.1, item 6). | NATIVE files are accessible across different ARITHMETIC options: a NUMERIC*4.2 field written under FIXED reads back as 12.35 under DECIMAL (FIX-0018) | FIX-0018 |
| 15.1.4 | D-15.1-7 | fixed | The way a value is rounded when it is assigned to a fixed-point variable with fewer fraction digits is not fixed by section 15.1.4, which only says it is rounded. | Half away from zero on the magnitude: LET A = -1.555 stores -1.56 and LET B = 1.555 stores 1.56 under *8.2 (FIX-0178); the same tie-break as the format items of PRINT USING (D-5.4-6). ROUND is different: it follows its normative formula INT(X*10^N+.5)/10^N, so ROUND(-1.555,2) is -1.55. | FIX-0178 |
| 15.2.2 | D-15.2.2-1 | fixed | Whether the ARITHMETIC options of two program-units joined by CHAIN must agree in fixed-point precision or only in type, and whether the numeric parameters of the program-name-line are subject to the ordering rule of OPTION ARITHMETIC FIXED. | Agreed interpretation of 15.2.2 (decision of the project owner, 2026-11-02): 15.2.2 l.12354-12357 only requires the ARITHMETIC options of the two program-units to agree in type (DECIMAL, NATIVE or FIXED), not in precision, so CHAIN from FIXED*4.2 to FIXED*8.2 executes without exception 4303 (SEG-0324); NATIVE vs DECIMAL still raise 4303 both ways (SEG-0311, SEG-0312). The ordering rule of 15.1.2 l.12145-12148 does not reach the parameters of the program-name-line (the first line), so a FIXED program with numeric program parameters is conforming. | SEG-0324, SEG-0311, SEG-0312 |

## 6. Enhancements over the standard

ANSI §2.2 (9) (l.553-556) requires the implementation to be accompanied by documentation that describes and identifies all enhancements to the language. A program that uses an enhancement is **not a conforming program** and is not portable to other implementations. The enhancements of this interpreter, each verified by its test, are:

| Clause | Claim ID | Module | Enhancement | Tests |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.2 | A-ENH-11 | core | Each external procedure keeps its own line-number sequence: an external unit may start below the end-line of the main program (120 END followed by 50 EXTERNAL SUB S) and may repeat line numbers used by the main program or by other units; order and uniqueness are still checked inside each program-unit and among the headers of the external units, and a line-number reference always reaches the line of its own unit (A-4.2.2-TR156). A conforming program uses unique line numbers in ascending order over the whole program. | ENH-0010 |
| 6.1 | A-ENH-1 | core | A unary sign is accepted right after a binary operator in a numeric expression (PRINT 2*-3 prints -6; also 1 - -3 = 4, - -3 = 3, 3 / +3 = 1). The sign applies to the operand that follows; the exponent still takes no sign (2^-1 is a syntax error). | ENH-0001 |
| 6.1 | A-ENH-2 | core | A program line holding only a line number (15, with neither REM nor a tail comment) is accepted as an empty line that does nothing; execution continues with the next line. The conforming form is 15 ! comment. | ENH-0002 |
| 6.1 | A-ENH-3 | graphics | In PLOT TEXT and GET POINT the initial-point may omit the comma before AT (PLOT TEXT AT 0.2, 0.7: "HI"; GET POINT AT 0.5, 0.5: X, Y gives X = 0.5, Y = 0.5); it behaves exactly as with the comma. | ENH-0003 |
| 6.1 | A-ENH-4 | files | SET #n: POINTER RECORD r and SET #n: POINTER KEY k$ are accepted and position the pointer exactly like the conforming enhanced setters SET #n: RECORD r and SET #n: KEY k$ (a following READ #n returns that record). | ENH-0004 |
| 6.1 | A-ENH-5 | files | REPLACE #n, RECORD r: item and MAT REPLACE #n, RECORD r: array are accepted and replace an existing record exactly like REWRITE / MAT REWRITE, including the phase-1 exceptions (7320 fatal on channel 0, 7322 fatal if the file is not OUTIN). | ENH-0005 |
| 6.1 | A-ENH-6 | files | NEXT #n advances the file pointer like SET #n: POINTER NEXT, and NEXT #n, setter positions the pointer like SET #n: <setter>; it does not collide with NEXT control-variable of a FOR loop. | ENH-0006 |
| 6.1 | A-ENH-7 | files | RANDOM #n RECORD k (without comma) positions the pointer at record k of a RELATIVE file, so a following READ #n returns that record; only RECORD is admitted as the argument. | ENH-0007 |
| 6.1 | A-ENH-8 | files | RENAME a$ TO b$ renames a file (7305 if the source does not exist, 7308 if the target already exists); after RENAME "a.dat" TO "b.dat" the content is readable under the new name. | ENH-0008 |
| 6.4 | A-ENH-10 | core | UCASE$(s$) and LCASE$(s$) return s$ with every letter converted to upper or lower case, including the Latin-1 letters (a-grave to thorn pair with A-grave to THORN, except the multiplication and division signs); sharp s and y-diaeresis have no one-character counterpart and stay unchanged. | ENH-0009 |
| 9.2.6 | A-ENH-9 | core | An internal SUB may be called before its definition, with no DECLARE SUB anywhere (100 CALL S / ... / 110 SUB S ... runs and prints; §9.2.6 l.4771-4773 lets an implementation accept an internal subprogram referenced before its definition). The portable conforming form is still DECLARE SUB before the first reference (SEG-0251). | SEG-0250 |

## 7. Not applicable

Claims that do not apply to this implementation, with the reason:

| Clause | Claim ID | Module | Claim | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1.3 | A-4.1.3-EX | core | The examples of the character section are declared empty, so no example program of section 4.1.3 needs to be accepted or run. | Section 4.1.3 declares 'Examples: None' (l.1124-1127), so there is no example program to accept or run. |
| 4.4.6 | A-4.4.6-01 | core | An implementation may add extra built-in functions, but a declaration of such a name in a program unit must override the built-in meaning there. | This implementation supplies no built-in functions beyond those of the standard (the parser's supplied-function lists match l.1885-1888 and the string list of 6.4), so there is no extra built-in whose meaning a declaration could override. |
| 4.4.6 | A-4.4.6-02 | core | An implementation offering parameterless enhancement functions must also give a syntax to tell them apart from plain variables, such as requiring a declaration or empty parentheses at each call. | No parameterless enhancement functions are supplied (the only no-argument supplied names are the standard's own reserved ones), so no distinguishing syntax is required. |
| 7.2.6 | E-1505 | core | Reporting an array expression underflow as exception 1505 is only a recommendation. | Table 9 lists 1505 as recommended and not mandated, so the standard requires no behaviour to test (the required behaviour, replacing the value by zero, is claim A-7.2.4.2-07). |
| 11.1.5 | E-7052 | files | Opening a device as a RELATIVE or KEYED file raises the fatal exception 7052. | The portable suite has a single device, the console on channel zero; OPEN on channel zero with any organization yields nonfatal 7002 (E-7002, FIL-0077) and NAME 'CONSOLE' creates a true file, so no device can be opened as RELATIVE/KEYED. Mandated at Table 9 l.12913. On POSIX hosts this interpreter also treats a file that is not regular (for example /dev/null) as a device and raises 7052; that is tested in FullBasicCoreXCTests/ComplianceFIOla2AXCTests. |
| 11.1.5 | E-7311 | files | ERASE on an OUTIN device without erase capability raises the nonfatal exception 7311: nothing is erased and execution continues. | The only device in the portable suite is the console on channel zero; ERASE on channel zero yields nonfatal 7002 (E-7002, FIL-0077), so 7311 cannot occur. Mandated at Table 9 l.12934. On POSIX hosts ERASE on a non-regular file opened with OUTIN (for example /dev/null) raises 7311, and ASK ERASABLE gives NO; that is tested in FullBasicCoreXCTests/ComplianceFIOla2AXCTests. |
| 11.2.5 | E-7205 | files | A record-setter on a device without that capability raises the nonfatal exception 7205: the pointer does not move and execution continues. | The only device is the console on channel zero, and any record-setter on channel zero yields nonfatal 7002 (E-7002, FIL-0077); no other device exists, so 7205 cannot occur. Mandated at Table 9 l.12919. |
| 11.4 | E-1508 | files | Treating a numeric underflow during file input as the nonfatal exception 1508 (supply zero and continue) is only recommended, not mandated, so no behaviour is required. | Table 9 l.12823 marks 1508 as recommended, not mandated ('I 1508'), and 11.4 l.8462 says 'is recommended'; the interpreter supplies zero without raising 1508. |
| 13.4.6 | E-8106 | graphics | Graphic input supplied outside the active window, the device window or the device viewport corresponds to exception code 8106. | Table 9 l.12993-12995 lists 8106 as 'recommended in the Remarks Section, and is not mandated', and 13.4.6 l.10383-10386 says 'It is recommended that...'; the interpreter accepts outside input (implementation-defined D-13.4-2), so no behaviour is required. |
| 14 | A-14-01 | core | Section 14 (Real Time) is not claimed: the interpreter does not implement real-time programs, parallel sections or event handling. | The real-time module is optional in ANSI X3.113-1987 (§2 (4), l.470-503) and does not exist in ECMA-116 (§2.5: real-time programs will not run on ECMA BASIC implementations); it is not implemented and not claimed. |
| 16 | A-16-01 | core | Section 16 (Editing) is not claimed as a module: the interpreter does not accept the editing commands (DELETE, EXTRACT, LIST, RENUMBER) as program text, and program lines must appear in increasing line-number order (claim A-4.2.2-04). | The editing module is optional in ANSI X3.113-1987 (§2 (6), l.470-503) and has no equivalent in ECMA-116; the host application's own source editor provides the editing functionality instead of the interpreter accepting the section 16 commands (project decision, 2026-10-20). |

## 8. Limits of the evidence

- **Self-declaration, not certification.** This document is published by the implementer. ANSI X3.113-1987 (FIPS PUB 68-2) defines conformance but does not certify implementations, and no external body has tested or endorsed this one: the claims are backed only by the programs listed above, run on the platform and at the commit identified in section 2.
- **What a program can prove.** That this interpreter accepts, rejects or executes each specific program with the specific result recorded, on that host. It cannot prove anything about programs not run, other hosts, platforms, operating-system versions or commits.
- **Real time (ANSI §14) is not claimed** and cannot be probed by this suite: no real-time programs, parallel sections or event handling are run (ANSI §14; ECMA-116 §2.5).
- **Editing (ANSI §16) is not claimed** as a module; editing is provided by the host application's editor, not by §16 commands in the program text (section 7).
- **Devices other than the console and files.** The command-line host exposes a single device, the console on channel zero, so exceptions that require another device (for example 7205 and 7311, Table 9 l.12919 and l.12934) cannot occur and are marked not applicable in section 7.
- **The wording of default exception reports** beyond the exception code and the line number is implementation-defined (§2.4 l.617-620); the tests check the code and the line, not the text around them.
- **Graphics** are compared through the interpreter's primitive trace (`--draw-log {drawlog}`), not by inspecting a rendered screen. The trace records the primitives, the window, viewport, clip, text-justify and color-mix settings and the values ASK returns, but not the line style, point style or color a primitive is drawn with, and it records the primitives before clipping, which the host renderer does: how each style and color looks, and the clipping itself, are checked only through ASK.
- **Resource-constraint exceptions** (§2.4 l.593-595) depend on the host's memory and limits; only the tested cases are claimed. Numeric precision and range are implementation-defined (Appendix C, §5.6) and are declared in section 5.
- **Absence is not evidence.** Clauses without a listed claim (the pending counts in the header and in section 3) are not a statement of non-conformance.
